sections.h:
The new house is established; the picture of Saint Anne is needed, and Vincenza should send it quickly. She is to welcome the two postulants, both good, and have them prepared; one can help the girls of the Poss factory in their spiritual formation and in running the Congregation of the Children of Mary established there. She is to record the postulants' accounts exactly and keep everything in order, because she must go and visit the house at Foligno.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your long letter through Sr. A. Paola. As for what you tell me about the postulant, do write that they should come and fetch her; you have done well in everything else too, [I am] very pleased.1

2. So, there is a house of the Daughters of Saint Anne here and the Chapel must soon be set up, and you will send me the picture of Saint Anne; have a small frame put on it, then put it in the crate and send it to the address of the Parish Priest [of] Vespolate that I sent you,2 as I have already given you; put inside the flower paper that Paola had left over, so that some flowers can be made here for this poor oratory, which has still to be set up.

3. Listen, you will receive this letter of mine from the hands of a 4th-grade certified teacher, a very dear person; I commend her warmly to you; give her a bed with a good mattress and curtains; she wishes to revise her studies a little. Let Sr. Anna Eletta take her on, have her revise them and give her good teaching; then we shall clothe her

soon; being with you she will learn and become a good religious; we may also be able to use her as a Superior.3

4. I hear about that person; he does well to enjoy himself.4 My dear Vincenza, there is as much work as one could want.

5. You are right that Providence does not seem to want to come to us through postulants. Listen, do write to the one from S. Arcangelo to bring the 1,000 F. in cash; explain yourself clearly, because, you know, sometimes these creatures bring in rags in place of money; not that; otherwise, let her come at once with 1,000 F. in cash and her outfit, cloth and linen, whatever she has.5

6. Be careful to note down well those postulants who still owe; have proper receipts made out on stamped paper with the date for this payment clearly fixed; do not forget, because unfortunately some of these hundred F. have gone astray.6 If a little store could be laid in for the winter, especially of grain and maize, enough. Let us pray, for the Lord will give us what we need.

7. So the Clothing can be performed by Father Mancini; and the one who comes with the teacher you will likewise put in a curtained bed, and she too will be clothed, for she will serve for Poss, for the girls' school, for spiritual matters, and likewise for the Children of Mary: she will encourage them, gather them, and you will see that the Congregation will be firmly founded; this pleases Mary and Saint Anne. You will clothe her and then put her to work; she will draw them.7

8. You must write to Soresina to send you girls, but let them see to it that they have a doctor's certificate that they are healthy and grown up; that is what you must look for; otherwise accept them; I shall try to do the same, and Poss may rest easy.8

9. See whether you could get that poor girl who came, from Piacenza, and whether she could be accepted; now she keeps coming to my mind; I am very sorry I sent her away. Have Mancini's girls not arrived yet?9

10. Address your letters to Ovada, but mind, I shall stay there only three days, so plan accordingly; you can send the exercise books and all the books so that she can study; but it is enough to send the picture with the flower things inside; that is enough; the rest will be brought by those who are to come later.10

11. My dear daughter, for charity's sake, try to get everything ready and in order, for as soon as Mancini comes, whom you will put in the Father's room, you will have to go to Foligno and also to S. Martinello, for things there are boiling over like a cauldron.11 First it would be neces-

sary for me to speak to you. Oh, how it pains me that you are tied down by the Holy Retreat, you cannot believe it! I am truly on thorns about Foligno, because it would be very good for you to leave at once, for no good would come of that Sup. knowing;12 enough, in person; it means you can come over here for a moment. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. R.

1 This letter has not been preserved. There is, however, the one of 18.9, in reply

to the present one.

2 Cf. L 320,3.

3 From the hands of a certified teacher. It cannot be determined precisely

from the Postulants' Register who she is.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza had informed her (on 11.9.74): “Fr Tornatore is going to the coun-

try today and will not be back until next Saturday”.

5 The one from S. Arcangelo: Margherita Casalini. When presenting her they said they

would pay F. 3,000, but then they had reduced the figure. They bring in

rags: they bring clothing of little value (rags) instead of money.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza gives her an account of the fees brought by the individual pos-

tulants (two of hers and seven of Fr Mancini's) and of how much they undertake to pay in later

instalments.

7 The clothing may be presided over by Fr Giovanni Mancini. (Cf. L 315,

n. 9). Likewise the young woman coming from Invorio with the teacher, mentioned above

in para. 3. She will be a good formator of the girls who work in the

Poss factory; she will draw them, guide them and encourage them in goodness.

8 you must write to the parish priest of Soresina, Fr Luigi Malfina, to send

girls for the Poss works, provided they have the requirements for

being taken on.

9 Mancini's girls arrived on 18 September.

10 To Invorio you can send, etc.; but it is enough: as for the other things, send

only the picture of Saint Anne and the paper for making flowers for the chapel.

11 Prepare in good time the welcome for Fr Mancini and everything else, because then

she will have to go to Foligno, where things are boiling like a cauldron under pressure, and

to S. Martinello.

12 She leaves the sentence unfinished. The explanation of the unpleasant situation

would be too long. She will speak to her about it.

She is at Ovada, where she will stay three days; she again commends the two postulants to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Here we are, arrived at Ovada, and on Monday morning [in Genoa] I hope to find letters from you there. I am still on my feet; please let that Person know that if he wants to write to me he should address the letters to Genoa, for I am sure he will write; I am not writing to him because I am tired of writing.1

2. Greet Carlotta for me; have the postulants reached you? I commend them both to you; I would like them to be happy, and the lame one to be able to write to the Bishop that she is happy; let her write wherever she likes. I hope she will write that she is happy; if that person comes, let him speak a little to both of them, especially to one.3 That is enough for now; I shall write to you at Genoa, where I hope to find letters from you. I am in a hurry, your

affectionate M.

1 Here we are: on the 18th they arrived at Ovada (Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega is with her);

on the 21st they will be in Genoa... let... know: the message is for Fr Tornatore.

2 the postulants from Invorio; to the Bishop of Novara, Mgr Giacomo Gentile.

3 Let Fr Tornatore speak to them a little and form them for religious life.

In two days she will be at Sampierdarena; she cannot tell her the exact time.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. God willing, on Monday I shall be in your arms; I shall get off at S. P. d'Arena on purpose;1 I cannot tell you the time because I want to go by way of Voltri, but I shall come to the Hospital as soon as I get off. I have received the newspaper; everything in person;2 I must go, for the carriage is here to take me to the Bishop at Strevi.3 I have been travelling since Monday; I am all of a heap.4

Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and believe me yours

Affectionately, M. R.

1 Monday, 21 September; I want to go by way of Voltri (near Genoa).

2 The newspaper: cf. L 316, n. 2.

3 I am going to the Bishop at Strevi (Alessandria).

4 all a heap of aches from great fatigue.

She instructs her to send two Sisters to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. God willing, on Monday I shall be at S. P. d'Arena and then Genoa.1 I am writing in haste: send Sr. A. Palmira and Sr. A. Virginia to Piacenza at once. I hope you will certainly send them on Monday, as this letter will reach you tomorrow.2

Greet everyone; I am

your affectionate M. R.

1 Cf. L 323,1.

2 She has Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti and Sr. A. Virginia

Gaggi leave for Piacenza at once.

She accepts his proposal to take on the schools and sets out certain indispensable conditions for acceptance.

Reverend Parish Priest,

1. Forgive me for not answering your most esteemed letter by return of post; the reason was my absence. I very willingly accept the direction of the schools that Your Very Reverend Lordship proposes to me.2

2. I need only let you know that we cannot go fewer than four, or three at the very least, and also that the stipend you propose is too little; it should be at least 1,200 f. If Your Reverence agrees to this, write to me the day on which I am to send them and I will send them to you at once.3

In the hope of a letter from you, whether confirming or declining, believe me, with all esteem and reverence,

Your most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The Mother was at Ovada, but was to go to Genoa on 21 September;

so she dated the letter from Genoa.

2 The direction of the Schools at Montefiorino (Modena).

3 write to me: she lets him understand that her answer is positive.

She encloses a letter for the Father, answers some of her questions and asks for prayers, from the community as well, for the conversion of a Priest who is in the Sampierdarena Hospital with a serious illness.

A.M.F. Dear daughter,

1. A line in haste; tomorrow I leave for Genoa, where I shall be at 12/13 in the afternoon. Write to me at the Genoa house. Today, as I write, you will have that Person there; give him this.2

2. You ask me about the postulant's brother, the Priest: yes, let him come and attend the ceremony.3

3. You tell me about the accounts. My God! Enough, I am at peace, everything will come to you.4

4. Has Carlotta gone to Genoa?5 Goodbye.

5. Greet everyone for me and have prayers said for the journey, and also a novena for the conversion of a Priest who is in the hospital at S. P. d'Arena, who became a Protestant and now has cancer of the tongue and will hear of nothing. I commend him to you earnestly; tell the postulants, the religious, that person; meanwhile, a novena.

6. This too, in silence, you will tell the person, about Foligno.6 Alas, dear Vincenza, what troubles there are! Enough, [I entrust myself] to our little mother of the Sacred Heart of Jesus; She will set everything right for me; and pray. Goodbye.

7. For charity's sake, let Carlotta not leave Onorata's side, and I would not like her to go to the Countess's alone.7

[Your affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

The date is deduced from the context.

On the 21st, Monday. Give the enclosed letter to Fr Tornatore. The brother of the Postulant Elena Merli, from Cortemaggiore. The clothing took place on 29 September.

4 the accounts. Vincenza had written to her on the 18th: “I gave the mason F. 200, but

how much there still is! The carpenter also gave me his account and it comes to F. 600”. The

Mother learns this with pain: my God! But she adds confidently: everything will

come to you, providence will come to pay it all.

5 She does not yet know anything definite about the departure. On 11 September Sr. A. Vin-

cenza had told her that they (Carlotta and Onorata Colli) would leave for

Genoa on 15 or 16 September.

6 You will tell Fr Tornatore, in secret, about the unpleasant situation at Foligno.

(Cf. L 321,11).

7 Carlotta was warmly received by Countess Edvige Marazzani and gladly

went to her palazzo.

She speaks of two girls to be sent to Genoa. At Cortemaggiore difficulties have arisen between the Hospital Administration and the two Communities. She asks her forgiveness for not having shown her all the attention she deserved, encourages her and invites her to join her in Genoa after pressing for the examinations to be held.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here we are at S. P. d'Arena; I am writing to you in my own hand so that you may be convinced that I am well and have had [a good journey]; it is very late and I am writing to you on my knees.

2. Listen: 1st, tell that person that I received his letter at Ovada; 2nd, see whether that girl from Genoa who was ill in the hospital, the one who was so naughty, if by ill luck she has come out and is not behaving, you could send her, and also that other one who is always poorly, send her away too, as she [is] from Genoa; you could send them to Sr. A. Elvira, for they need them here.2

3. Patience, I made a mistake; what can I say? my dear, I am a dolt. The father of the postulant you wrote to brought us F. 40, which I am keeping.3

4. Give this letter from Insani to that Person, but tell him it is not true that Sr. A. Tina wants money and said he should have it asked of me.4 Enough; do you know what has happened meanwhile? They made it known that the Superior of the hospital helps the other, and so

the Administration raised an uproar without equal and the village is saying all sorts of things,5 and in the hospital they now want only 4 Sisters, and moreover the hospital Sisters are no longer to go to those at the Maddalena, and those cannot go to the hospital any more, and a fine mess has been made of it. My God!6

5. Dear Vincenza, you know, I have a scruple at having always been so disobliging to you; you showed me a thousand attentions and I always mortified you. How I suffer for this courtesy of mine, God alone sees; meanwhile I ask your forgiveness and hope with God's help never to do such things again.7

6. Yes, clothe all those you think fit, for I shall always approve everything.8 Do everything with courage and do not fret. When you have held the clothing, come to Genoa; I shall write to tell you whom to bring me.

7. Listen, see about pressing for the examinations, because I would need to send them by the middle of October. Ask the Inspector, and the Priest too, to whom I hope you will have sent the present.9

8. I would like you to give French lessons to Sr. A. Eletta, because I must send her as teacher to Invorio; but silence, for charity's sake, let no one know; I hope a few lessons will be enough for her. The Superior Sr. Filomena will come to you and you will put her at the Morte,10 so that Sr. A. Eufemia will be free, for she will have to leave as soon as she has taken her examinations.11

Goodbye, yours in haste, affectionately for ever,

MOTHER ROSA. Address your letters to Genoa.

1 The date is incomplete, but the month and year are easily identified from the

content.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza replies (on 23.9) that she will send them both to

Genoa, accompanied by Sr. A. Elvira Persiani.

3 I made a mistake... Reading these expressions and the others in para. 5, her daughter

is astonished: “My Mother, whatever is this! you were not yourself when you wrote such things. My

God, I who caused you so much grief, ah, if you could feel the pain it gives me!”.

4 you will give Canon Stefano Insani's letter to Fr Tornatore.

5 Cf. L 328, n. 3 and 4.

6 those at the Maddalena: the Sisters of the other community, devoted to nursing

the sick at home, who are guests of Signora Maddalena Parmigiani. Cf.

L 328.

7 always disobliging: I did not know how to repay you, I was ungrateful;

how I suffer for this discourteous way of behaving.

8 The clothing took place at the end of the Spiritual Exercises preached by

Fr Mancini (L Sr. A. Vincenza to M. Rosa, 23.9.74), on 29 September.

9 The examinations were held on 20 October (cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 1.10.74).

And the Priest: presumably a member of the Board.

10 Sup. Filomena Pugnaloni is assigned to the house in Via della Morte.

11 Sr. A. Eufemia Camporesi was to complete her studies in preparation

for the teaching certificate examinations.

She has been informed of their displeasure at the two supernumerary Sisters in the Hospital. She explains her reasons and assures them she has withdrawn them.

[Mr President]2

1. I have received letters from the Superior informing me that Your Most Illustrious Lordships are displeased at having more Sisters in your Hospital (than) the agreed number.3 I did this so that the patients might be better cared for and the Sisters more relieved of fatigue; it was, moreover, a gift that the Daughters of Saint Anne were making to this Hospital entirely at their own expense.

2. Since Your Most Illustrious Lordships do not welcome this – whereas all the other Hospitals would ask nothing better than that we increase the Sisters at our expense – I have already ordered the said Superior to send the two extra Sisters to Piacenza, and likewise to cut off communication between Signora Maddalena's house and the Hospital.4

3. I would ask the Administration kindly to send me a line for my guidance. Please accept the sentiments of deep esteem and respect of one who is honoured to call herself Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 President of the hospital, Signor Luigi Parmigiani.

3 The Superior Tommasina Viterbo had informed her on 15 Septem-

ber of the complaint made to her about the excess number of Sisters: six instead of the four

required by the contract.

4 cut off communication: the said Superior also told her of

another cause of discontent: “in the village they say that the Sisters (of the other commu-

nity) come and eat the hospital's food, and if I sometimes send them some-

thing they say I keep them on the hospital's goods”.

3-

O

Cortemaggiore – Hospital: a ward.

From her letter she hears how providence is helping her. She is pleased with the good news about Fr Mancini; tell him to call the Daughters of Saint Anne to Paris. Two chasubles must be sent to Invorio. She has much work, but plans to go to Piacenza at the end of the month for just two days. She needs to speak to her before sending her to Terricciola and S. Martinello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter and hear how providence is helping you; I hope you will pay the accounts; by now you will have received my second letter, in which I sent you Insani's, and you will have heard how the muddle happened; enough. God, I hope, will put it right.1

2. I am very glad of the good news you give me of Father Mancini; tell him to call us to Paris; I approve all you have done, you do everything well; courage, and do not go about things fearfully.2

3. I have not even time to breathe, so weighed down am I with work; do not think I do this for any other reason, because if you saw me you would certainly be dumbfounded. Perhaps on Monday you can manage it: send the old red chasuble, the one I had repaired, which is spare, and also the old white one, which is spare, to Invorio Inferiore, to the Superior; I am sending the rest from here.3

4. Goodbye, I have too much work. “My God, give me a hundred arms, that I may wear them all out for you”.4

5. Probably at the end of October I shall slip away to

Piacenza for 48 hours, without saying anything. There are too many things I must tell you, and you must go to Terricciola and S. Martinello.5

Your affectionate M. R. Many greetings to all. Goodbye, my dear.

1 your letter: it is dated 23.9.74; providence is helping you. There had been an in-

come of 800 F. My second: L 327.

2 “Fr Mancini is ever more enthusiastic about the Daughters of Saint Anne and is so

happy here... he says he feels he is in Paradise... he says he could listen to us

praying for ever.” He – writes Vincenza – was about to go to Paris.

3 Perhaps on Monday you can manage it: send to the Superior Paola Buc-

ciotti at Invorio the red and the white chasubles that are spare, which we do not

need.

4 My God... for you: a concise and telling expression.

5 To Terricciola (Pisa) and S. Martinello – Perugia, two communities that were

to be opened.

She instructs her to send two nurses to Rome and also to send an alb to Invorio, where the Bishop wants the clothing of the six postulants to take place. She has an eye infection and finds it hard to write.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today, a minute's time after writing eight letters, so that I can no1 longer even feel my stomach. I still need to write to you to tell you many things. Listen, for charity's sake, send two nurses to Rome quickly: Sr. A. Geltrude – if she is better – and Sr. A. Cunegonda. If Geltrude is not well, then replace her with another from Cortemaggiore, but not from Maddalena's house,2 rather from the hospital, and a good one. Signora Elisa will go too.

2. You would need to send, do send an alb to Invorio; the rest, corporals, amices, etc., I am sending from here.3

3. Listen, you would need to send her the form for the clothing, because the Bishop wishes to clothe those six at Invorio, where they are now; then they will send them straight back to Piacenza and you will send them others. I shall let you know beforehand.4

4. I would like to write to that person, but my God! I do not know where my head is. I am going to Mamma, for they are saying Mass for the first time, and then I must be at the meeting about S. P. d'Arena.6

5. My eyes are very bad; this is the 12th letter I have written this morning alone; what is happening to me I do not know; they

hurt and give off a great deal of matter. I hope I shall soon be better. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me and believe me, in haste, your affectionate

M. R.

1 nemo: not even.

2 Sr. A. Geltrude Gottelli and Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti. Maddalena's house:

cf. L 327, n. 6.

3 Cf. L 329,3.

4 The Bishop, Mgr Giacomo Gentile. (Cf. L 322, n. 2).

5 for they are saying Mass for the first time in the house chapel.

6 at Sampierdarena she was to attend a meeting with the hospital

administrators.

Worried about her illness, she asks for news of her health and urges her to take care of herself. Vincenza has paid the debts, which pleases her. Prudence in speaking of the house's finances. She tells her the price of flour in Genoa, for her guidance.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hear from your letter that you have had convulsions; however did it happen? What was the cause? Ah, for pity's sake, write and tell me whether the air there is making you suffer.

2. I am glad to hear that you have paid all the accounts; for charity's sake, try to eat, and drink a little wine.

3. You did well to answer that person so, and if she comes again to ask you such questions, tell her: “Madam, rest assured that I have already paid them all, and so I no longer need to talk about it”. For pity's sake, be careful, because it is a very serious matter.1

4. As for the wine, I am glad the Countess provides it for you, because it is an expense not known about.2 Flour is now very cheap;3 here the finest flour costs only F. 38 a sack, which is a quintal; this for your guidance. For charity's sake, take care of yourself, I urge you.

Goodbye; you will soon have the teacher, and I am your

affectionate M. R.

1 Signora Teresina Zagotti had asked her for “the amount of the debt, tel-

ling me that the Countess wanted to know it” – so the Superior – and she, remembering

the Mother's warning, told her nothing (cf. L 319,4).

2 an expense not known about: it is not clear what she means; perhaps not fore-

seeable.

3 Flour is cheap.

Mgr Negrotto was unfavourably impressed by the Poss factory; he may be told that everyone is enthusiastic, that many girls are on the list to start work and that much good is done there. She asks whether he has been able to cash the vouchers of two postulants. She hopes also to receive news of the Marchioness Anguissola, who is visiting Rome.

A.M.F.

My Father Agostino,

1. A minute's time, in haste, I devote entirely to you, for it seems a century since I had letters from you, and since I wrote to you. I do not know how the Poss factory made such an impression [on] Mgr N.;2 well, you can tell him that, on the contrary, everyone is very enthusiastic, and I do not know which of the first applicants to accept, and many are waiting for a place. Good is being done; it happened that the factory was empty, so it made no impression;3 enough, let us leave everything in God's hands; let Him see to what He wants in His Work.

2. Tell me whether you have been able to check the vouchers of those two; I would like to hear that they have been cashed; then you could hand them over to Sr. A. Domenica.4

3. I hope soon to receive letters from you bringing good news. I gather that you will now be tireless on behalf of the Marchioness Anguissola; who knows how many dinners you will already have enjoyed; the Archpriest will keep you good company, and the Pope will have received her with pleasure, and Mgr N. Enough, write and tell me everything, for I am anxious for news.5

Receive a sackful of greetings from all, and in particular from one who calls herself Yours for ever,

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is deduced from Fr Agostino's reply, which acknowledges receipt

on 29 September.

2 Mgr Augusto Negrotto, after visiting the houses of Genoa and Sampier-

darena, went to Piacenza and there visited the two houses and the Poss factory. But here

he was not favourably impressed (cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 28.9.1874).

3 I do not know which of the first to accept: there are so many applications from

girls that she does not know whom to prefer.

4 The vouchers: of Sr. A. Elvira Persiani and Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni, two

Sisters from Rome; the Superior Domenica Marchesini.

5 The Marchioness Fanny Anguissola had gone to Rome with the Archpriest of

Cortemaggiore, Fr Domenico Costa. Mgr N.: Negrotto.

She has had no letters for days and fears for Vincenza's health. The two little girls and Sr. A. Filomena will have arrived. She reminds her to send Sr. A. Paola the Rules for the Confessor. Her eyes are still very bad and she has a great deal of work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For three days I have [received] no letters from you; I want to hope that it is as I think, that you are very busy; meanwhile the fear that it is your health will not leave me; enough.1

2. Today you will have received the two little girls, very good and hard-working, small but sturdy, and also Sr. A. Filomena, who will afterwards serve for the house of the Morte.2

3. You forgot to send Sr. A. Paola the Rules for the Confessor. See whether you are still in time; it would be good to put them in the crate with the chasubles. For charity's sake, let them not go astray.3

4. Have you sent the two nurses to Rome? Has that person come back from the country?4

5. My dear Vincenza, how much work! I do not know where I am; besides, my eyes are still very bad: all the wicked thoughts coming out through the eyelids. I write, but I assure you that in the evening it feels as if there were lots of pins in them.5 I must finish, because I am going to S. P. d'Arena, but I shall be back this evening. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me and believe me your

affectionate MOTHER 609

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had been very busy with the clothing of the postulants

(cf. L 327, n. 8).

2 Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni: she went as Superior to the house in Via della

Morte (cf. L 327, n. 10).

3 to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, the Superior of the newly opened house at Invorio

Inferiore (cf. L 320,1-3; 329,3).

4 Cf. L 330,1. That person: Fr Tornatore.

5 the wicked thoughts coming out through the eyelids: a jovial way of making light

of that ailment, which was no small matter; cf. L 330,5.

Worried about her health, she advises her to call the doctor, not to worry about debts and to ask her for whatever she needs. She need not trouble herself about the Countess: she is given a present only for Saint Anne's day. In any case, the Mother will let her know if anything needs doing.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received a letter from you in which you tell me you are still poorly. How it grieves me! You certainly cannot believe it, and besides, the convulsion you had keeps me in constant anxiety.2 Have you called the doctor? Listen, for pity's sake, do not go distressing yourself over the debts, because if you have no [money] I will send you some.3

2. Write and tell me, and I will send you at once whatever you need, but for pity's sake do not be upset. Write to me at once how you are; and as for Sr. A. Luigia, I shall soon remove her from you; say nothing; then you will put Sr. A. Costantina in her place and you will see she does well. All this when I send you the teachers.4

3. Do not worry about the Countess, because it was never the custom to send her anything, only on Saint Anne's day, because it is her name day. At Christmas only a letter and nothing else, do you understand? So rest easy, for if there were anything to be done I would tell you.

4. Be careful to go and pay a visit to His Eminence before he goes to Rome.5 Goodbye, in haste,

your affectionate M.

1 this must be a slip: September has 30 days.

2 Cf. L 331,1.

3 do not go distressing yourself. Sr. A. Carlotta had set herself “with great determination

and even at the cost of her life to set everything right, and perhaps this has affected her

health” – these are the exact words written to the Mother – on 28 September.

4 She has thought of removing a Sister who causes her trouble in the community.

5 His Eminence the Cardinal Protector, Luigi Vannicelli.

She acknowledges her letters and tells her that in a week she will be at Piacenza, together with Sr. A. Benedetta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received all your letters and now the last, in which you tell me you have sent the two religious to Rome.1 Listen, as for the programme, it was to be sent to Palo; what can I say, it is a [...].2 Listen, on Saturday I hope to be at Piacenza, so everything in person. Anna is here with me and says she is coming with me to Piacenza on Saturday.3 I write little because I have no time.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me and believe me your affectionate

M. R.

1 Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti and Sr. A. Cristina Marchelli.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza had asked her for an explanation of this, but the Mother re-

plies that she will tell her everything on her return to Piacenza and leaves the sentence unfinished; cf. L

336,1.

3 Anna Carrega also arrives with the Mother on Saturday 10 October.

[The] Cardinal Antonucci wants the Rules before we go into his diocese. Vincenza is to speak to the Father about it and send them as soon as possible with a letter. She is to make sure the examinations take place on the 20th, because the Sisters must leave.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For fear I did not write to you what I am about to tell you, with my poor head in a thousand affairs, not to say an abyss of things, and my brain very small. Listen, Cardinal Antonucci, Bishop of Ancona, wants the Rules before we go there, so as to allow us to go into his diocese – it is that programme I had you write to send to the Parish Priest of Palo, diocese of Ancona – so I was at ease thinking I had written to you to send these Rules.1

2. You will speak of it to that person; I have no time to write to him, there are too many things I want to do these days.2

3. So have them bound in red and send them to him; the address (and) on top, with a little ribbon inside, well wrapped and then secured with another band, and a courteous letter saying that we shall be most happy to lend our most wretched labour in his diocese and to be under his protection.3

4. Ask that person what he thinks; it seems to me that refusing them would be a mistake, and who knows what they might say. So try to do it at once, because I fear I have already delayed too long. Patience, the effect of my memory.4

5. Make quite sure the examinations are held by the twentieth, because

they must leave, it being already late.5 Goodbye, we shall see each other on Saturday, your

6. I was forgetting the other thing: listen, send two bottles of the Holy Father's wine to the President at Ovada; on the neck of one write, on a tied label, “For Fr Tito”; and a line to the President asking him to accept the bottle.6

1 She clarifies what she had not explained well in the previous letter. Sr. A. Vin-

cenza replies that she has understood; she is to send the Rules to the Parish Priest Bianchi. There

had been negotiations with him: cf. L 286 and 293. The place was Polverigi and not, as

was written by a slip, Palo, a village that does not exist in the diocese of Ancona.

Cardinal Benedetto Antonio Antonucci replied that he had received the rules, on

28.10.1874 (AFSA, F59).

2 You will speak of it to Fr Tornatore and hear his opinion.

3 Precise directions on how to send the Rules by post; she does not over-

look the gist of the covering letter.

4 Try to carry out the above at once; there has already been delay through her

forgetfulness.

5 The Sisters' certificate examinations (cf. L 327, n. 9).

6 The bottles of the Holy Father's wine, to be precise from the vineyard of the Parroc-

chietta, owned by the Vatican. One bottle to the President, Marco Montano,

with a little note, and one to Fr Tito Borgatta.

She is glad to read good news of her health. She urges her to ask for whatever she needs and to be cheerful. She asks her to send all of Sr. A. Paola's things to Invorio.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste: I have received yours and am glad to hear you are better; take care of yourself, for pity's sake, do not go distressing yourself, for you have only to write to me and I will send you everything you need.

2. Meanwhile, do me the kindness of sending Paola's things to this address, everything, as well as her letters and books that you see belonged to her; winter clothes, in short everything. The address is: Arona, for Invorio Inferiore.1 Be cheerful, my daughter, for charity's sake. Courage and patience! Send the things without paying anything. Goodbye; and by slow goods service, but write to her that you have sent them and send her the consignment note.2

Yours in haste,

affectionately, M. R.

1 The things of Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, whom she had replaced, had remained at

Ferrara. She is to send everything to Invorio Inferiore. Cf. L 333, n. 3.

2 without paying anything: with carriage charged to the addressee, so as

not to burden the meagre finances of the Ferrara house.

She thanks him for the forms he sent. Her indulgenced Crucifix has been stolen, and she asks him to get her another. She will soon send the two Sisters. She regrets the obstacles placed in the way of the service of charity. It is time to work, but unfortunately she can do very little, in such poor health as she is.

A.M.F.

My Father,

1. I have received yours with the forms enclosed, for drawing those small dowries. May the Lord bless you, who work for the Daughters of Saint Anne.1 On Saturday I go to Piacenza and shall at once have my signature authenticated by the Curia, because, as you know, here it is not within our reach. My Father, on every side there are sorrows and troubles; if God so wills, may He be blessed for ever.

2. Listen, while travelling, I do not know how, some zealous creatures stole my Crucifix, and it grieves me, because it had the indulgences for the Way of the Cross, so I can no longer make it, since being lame I cannot walk round. My Father Agostino, buy me another and have these words written on the cross: Via Crucis: privileged blessing in articulo mortis – then perhaps they will be moved and not steal it from me. I had all the Religious questioned and it was not they.2

3. I shall soon send the teacher for the Fornaci and the Superior for the Parrocchietta. I hope they will do good; otherwise those poor girls might fall into the hands of lay teachers and turn from dear Children of Mary into devils.

4. How it grieves me always to hear that to do a little good one needs comforts!3

5. “My Saviour! You who preached in the open, you without house or roof, had nothing but the glorification of your Father; and we?”.4

6. Poor me, a real little dolt, I have never been able to do anything for this dear Redeemer; it is time to toil! I am sorry that I can do nothing myself, being always poorly; indeed, from getting caught in the rain I have a cough of no small account.5

7. Could it be the signal to retire? Enough, let us leave it to God; all He does is always for our good.6 Pray for me, as I do for you.

Your humble Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 the forms: the forms for drawing the small dowries of two Sisters, which he had

been seeing to. (Cf. L 332, n. 4).

2 I had the religious questioned one by one; none of them took it.

3 how it grieves me to hear of the obstacles raised and the com-

forts required in order to do a little good.

4 Jesus teaches us otherwise. She turns to Him, poor and itinerant, moved

solely by the glorification of the Father (Lk 9:57-58). And we? The contrast is

stark.

5 Poor me. She feels she has pointed out others' shortcomings and looks at her-

self: I can do nothing... merely from being caught in the rain, she has a cough

of no small account.

6 to retire? ...good. Filial abandonment to God the Father, lived in the sad

and joyful events of daily life, keeps her ready to welcome the final call

with a trusting “here I am” in His mercy.

Having set out the aims and manner of running her charitable work, which is strictly private in character, she disputes the attempt to treat the house at Sampierdarena as an Opera Pia, subject to the regulations governing such Works. She therefore asks for a ruling on the nature of this Home for poor girls, so that she can take the appropriate decisions.

[Most Illustrious Prefect],

1. The undersigned, moved by the desire to be of some use to suffering humanity, gathered around her a number of women able to assist her in her aims with their means, their intelligence and their good will.

2. The Work, begun some years ago, is making progress with the approval of a great many families, for the aim of the petitioner and her companions is: 1st, to care for the sick in the families where they are called for; 2nd, to take in poor girls who are orphaned or abandoned, to give them a moral education and teach them women's crafts, for a small fee or even free of charge.

3. The petitioner meets all expenses and needs from her own means, without recourse either to public charity or to any of the other sources on which Charitable Institutions depend, whether founded through the virtue and generosity of a pious founder or on the initiative of benevolent citizens.

4. The petitioner does not intend to give her charitable works a public character; she lives privately with her companions, and each provides from her own funds for her individual

needs or those shared with the others. She asks nothing of the Government but the personal protection to which she is entitled as a citizen and taxpayer of the State, whose laws she respects.

5. In this social condition of hers, which is contrary to no law, she cannot understand why the provisions of the law on Opere Pie should be applied to the group of girls whom she supports with her own money and the help of her friends, in premises she owns at Sampierdarena.

6. She believes she is not bound to give account of her actions so long as they are not contrary to the principles of public morality and the laws of the State. Should the Government wish to compel her to submit to government supervision, she would be obliged, in order to preserve her freedom, to abandon to poverty and the dangers of corruption the many poor girls whom the undersigned has so far supported and cared for with her own means.

7. The petitioner therefore begs Your Excellency to declare definitively whether the Home for girls at Sampierdarena under the title – Daughters of Saint Anne – is or is not a Charitable Institution subject to the law on Opere Pie, so that the petitioner may decide whether or not to continue the work she has undertaken.

The Petitioner ROSA GATTORNO

1 The Prefect's name has been taken from historical documents of the period.

She answers her letter at once to reassure her. She reminds her of her promise never to go out alone and to take part in community prayer. Without prayer, work is imperfect. If Francesca loves her, as she has so often shown in deeds, she must confirm it by giving proof of a great love for God.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter, and to reassure you I am writing at once; I am a little better; the cough that still torments me will, let us hope, stop.1 My dear Francesca, remember the promise you made me never to go about alone, and also to see that the Sisters never go about alone.2

2. You promised me that you would pray and be present at the Community prayers. Yes, my dear, prayers are the adornment of our actions; what happens if we offer our God imperfect work? He will surely set it aside and not even look at it; but if it is adorned and embellished by prayer, then indeed it will draw His gaze, and He will take pleasure in us.3

3. Ah, bliss beyond compare, that we should be God's delight! Ah, my daughter, what joy; there is nothing on this earth like it.4

4. You told me so many times, and showed me in deeds, your love for me, for which I am exceedingly grateful to you; but how happy I would be if you confirmed it by giving me proof that you love God greatly and feel a great love for Him; I assure you

that this joy would be a great relief to me in my burdens.5

5. Come, then, come with me to Calvary for love of our Crucified One, to be for Him alone and with Him on the Cross!6

Greet the Sisters for me, the two dentists7 and Sr. A. Elisabetta; and receive many good wishes from one who calls herself your

affectionate M. R.

1 She had a cough from being caught in the rain (cf. L 338,6).

2 It was a prescription of the Rule not to go out alone, but always with

another Sister.

3 you will pray and be present at the community prayers. She has asked her for a pro-

mise of fundamental importance: she must pray, because prayer fills actions

with the divine; she will be present...: the Superior, mother and guide, is always and

first of all within the praying community, a sign of unity and communion.

4 to be God's delight is for the Mother the bliss that infinitely surpasses

every joy that can be tasted on earth.

5 One more recommendation, pressing and closely reasoned: you have told

me and shown in deeds that you love me; how happy I would be if you confirmed it

with proof that you love God greatly...

6 The final invitation: come with me. She cannot lead her elsewhere, because her way

is that of our crucified Love.

7 The two Sisters, dentists and nurses, who did a great deal of good: Sr. A.

Candida Carboneschi and Sr. A. Innocenza Dimari (cf. L 287, n. 6); Sr. A. Elisabetta

Veronesi.

The teacher wants to go home; very well, let her read what is written here, then let her leave for Piacenza accompanied by a Sister. A replacement will be sent. She urges her to accept with courage what the Lord sends us.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter; I hear about the teacher;1 well then – listen, you will tell her that – or rather, you will read her these two lines.

2. Listen, you wish to leave, and I will most willingly have you accompanied at once without delay; be so good as to leave on Monday morning, and as soon as you arrive here I will hand you your things, so that you can go home without any more crosses or fears. There, everything is settled, in holy peace, without fuss; I am ready at once; I only regret the commotion you made, and certainly the scandal you have given with your unkind and despairing words; enough. God bless you.2

3. Listen, then be sure to send her accompanied by Sr. A. Luigia, and wait until the Countess has gone. I will send you another, only you must keep an eye on her so that she does not speak to any of the Countess's people.3

4. For charity's sake, my daughter, what can you expect; you must know that she is a poor creature without a penny, who lived in a wretched room together with a peasant woman. You see, she had neither servants nor menservants, but poverty, poverty!

5. Courage, my dear daughter; everything God sends us is always for our good, so that we may gain ever more merit.4

For charity's sake, despise this wretched worldly one, which is nothing but a handful of dust to be despised.5 Goodbye, it is late. Believe me yours for ever,

affectionately, M. ROSA

1 The Superior had written to her: “Diomira Piccini (she had taken the religious habit

on 29 September 1874) has taken to her bed saying that the air does not suit her, and

she keeps growing more dejected, declaring that religious life is not for her

... her home, her servants, her comforts are always on her lips... The Sis-

ters vie with each other in being kind to her, but even so we cannot persuade her

to start the school”. The Mother intervenes with a firm and timely decision.

2 I only regret the scandal she has given the community.

3 Wait until she has gone: the Countess was to leave in two days. It was

prudent not to speak of it with the Countess's retinue, to avoid com-

ment and remarks.

4 Courage... it had been a bad experience for the Superior too, who was new

to the house.

5 ...this wretched worldly one. At this point there is a note on the letter in

the hand of Father A. M. Fiocchi: after the word wretched he wrote “a word is certainly missing

here, e.g. life, and it certainly does not refer to the person mentioned above”. It should

then be understood: despise this wretched worldly life, which is nothing but...

She has received her consoling letter and the basket. After 1 November she will send some religious and explains what is to be done for them. She asks her to pray for Sr. A. Vincenza's health. She has much work with the Clothing of four postulants. She orders a pair of dental forceps.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter,1 which consoled me not a little, and the basket too. Listen, I do not want you always spending money on me, when you are in such great need yourselves.

2. Listen, I would have written when I sent you that religious, but that evening my head would no longer hold up; you will have understood that she was for you, to take the place of the one from Ferentino; so send the latter to Genoa, where she was before.2

3. Listen, after All Souls' Day I will send you one from Cortemaggiore whom I would like you to teach, and at the same time try to steady a little; I cannot make anything of her ideas.3 See what you think; the other, who will be her companion, will be for Genoa. Perhaps, if I can, I shall send two; I shall see.

4. I have written to the one at Sestri to try to repay you those F. 25, because I know she had them, as Signora Morando left them to us.4 I rely on your promise in all you tell me, for charity's sake.

5. Sr. A. Vincenza has been in bed since Saturday with bronchitis; today she is a little better, but I am not yet satisfied, be-

cause she still has a fever. Have some prayers said that she may soon be up.

6. Goodbye, yours in haste, because we have work beyond compare: on Sunday, All Saints' Day, four more postulants are to be clothed.

7. Greet everyone for me; I would like the Director to order me a key for extracting teeth, at my expense, like the one he ordered for Sr. A. Candida.5

God bless you together with all, whom I greet, and I remain your

affectionate M.

1 The letter being answered has not been preserved.

2 that religious... the one from Ferentino: further information is lacking to identify

the persons; so send her: it is understood that the one from Ferentino is to be sent back

to Genoa.

3 one from Cortemaggiore: Sr. A. Elena Guglielmi, from the last clothing.

4 The one: the Superior of Sestri, Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi. Signora Nina

Morando, a friend of Mother Rosa and benefactress of the Sisters.

at my expense.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to encourage you to persevere in your holy resolutions and to ask God every day for holy perseverance. Oh, daughter, what a grace that is!

2. Your little letter consoled me; now I await another bringing me lots of good news about the examinations and the visit to the Pope; a kiss for me on his dear and holy hand, a blessing;2 in short, you are fortunate; and go on making yourself loved by Mgr N., with whom you will certainly be content, for he is a worthy prelate. Tell him I am vexed because he did not keep his promise to come, and give him my warm regards.3

Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me

your affectionate M. R.

1 The date is reckoned from that of the letter being answered.

2 Your little letter. Having arrived in Rome, at the Fornaci House, a few days before,

she wrote to M. Rosa about the journey and the visit to the Pope.

3 Mgr N.: Mgr Augusto Negrotto. Cf. L 71, n. 3. Tell him that... regards. He had

visited the communities of Genoa, Sampierdarena and Piacenza while the

Mother was visiting the communities of Nizza Monf. and Ovada.

She urges her to persevere in her holy resolutions of faithfulness to God. She awaits another letter with consoling news of the visit to the Pope. She urges her to make herself loved by Mgr Negrotto and to greet him on her behalf.

She tells her of the arrival of two nursing Sisters and urges her to see to the Sisters' instruction, the observance and the reading of the Rules.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you two nurses; the older one is very good, an angel, very good with the sick; try always to send the young one with an older one, because although she does well, she is not to be relied on yet;1 I urge you to receive the reports every day and also to hold the school for nursing.2 I shall soon send you others.

2. Thank you for the fine mushrooms you sent me; I have sent these two Sisters' things all in one sack to S. P. d'Arena; send for them.3

3. Be sure never to go out, for charity's sake, neither alone nor with the girl;4 read the Rules at table every day until you see that they know them by heart.5 For charity's sake, do not leave the book about, lest the religious take it into their heads to copy it, because that is not allowed. It is late.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you all, and believe me your

affectionate M.

4. Try to accompany Sr. A. Guglielma6 to

S. P. d'Arena this evening or tomorrow morning, as you think best.

I fear it may be too late; tonight she can sleep in Genoa and

tomorrow you will accompany her; yours.

1 They are two from the last clothing (29 September); they need to gain

experience of religious life and charitable service; she is not to be relied on: she must be

followed and guided.

2 The Sisters' reports on the home nursing they have done, and the in-

formation she gathers personally from those they have cared for. The school...

Cf. L 353, n. 3.

3 the things of the two Sisters mentioned above.

4 never to go out alone: cf. L 340, n. 2.

5 The Rules: cf. L 294,4. Do not leave the book about, so that the Re-

ligious do not feel the urge to copy them.

6 Sr. A. Guglielma Merli.

On behalf of a Canon of Piacenza she asks her to inquire at the Salesian Institute about the conditions of admission, the treatment, the fees and the trade qualification obtained there. She authorizes her to transfer Sisters from the Genoa House to the Sampierdarena Hospital.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received a letter from you; I hear you are keeping the key with you; I warn you that I shall soon need Sr. A. Battistina.2 I hear you say that I do not write to you, when on the contrary it was I who was owed a reply from you.

2. Listen, yesterday Canon Giacoboni3 came to ask me to write to you, so that you might do him a favour: to go to Don Bosco's house at S. P. d'Arena and tell them there is a well-to-do person who would like to place his boy there as a paying boarder, and would like to know what they give them to eat and how they treat them; he would like him to learn not book studies but a trade, and he would be willing to pay F. 20 a month for board; what they teach them; and they would like this at once, all these things clearly explained, what their timetable is.

3. You tell me there are ten at Sestri; well, I shall soon take some away, because I need them. What a business; it seems odd that these outsiders are all alike, understanding nothing and wanting to poke their noses into everything.4

4. I will not write at greater length, because I am alone at the desk and in

running the house; today I have a bad headache, and I am writing to you with my head bandaged.

5. For charity's sake, if you need Sisters, go to Genoa and take some, for there are 25 there and there is never a good one among them.5 Goodbye, dear Francesca, I am yours; tell the Sisters to pray that I may not have to take oaths and that we may win the lawsuit.6 Goodbye. Oh, how this matter pains me!

[your affectionate MOTHER]

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 The key: the dental forceps. (Cf. L 342,7).

3 Canon Pietro Giacoboni.

4 there are ten at Sestri. This is news Francesca had received, evidently

from an outsider, which is why M. Rosa makes this remark.

5 If you need Sisters trained for the hospital, among 25 there cannot fail

to be a capable one.

6 to take oaths: to testify in court under oath. The Ricchini

lawsuit is still pending and causes her great distress.

She thanks him for the invitation to take on a school and sets out the conditions that stand in the way of accepting it.

Most Illustrious Count Raffaele Emaldi,

1. I have received your most esteemed letter and hasten to reply, first to thank you for the concern you show for us.2

2. Allow me to point out that five religious cannot live on the meagre allowance of twelve hundred francs, nor can they support a maidservant; but it means that four religious will be able – as in other places – to do everything, fulfil the government requirements and also satisfy the Congregation.

3. Allow me further to state more explicitly in writing that I absolutely cannot accept that lay teacher living with us; in that case I could not accept the direction of those schools, since it is forbidden in our Constitutions.

Please accept the sincere respects of one who has the honour to sign herself, Count,

your most devoted Servant, Sister A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 It is assigned to this period on the basis of how the request developed.

2 He had asked her for Sisters to direct a Girls' School at

Lugo di Ravenna.

As the Sisters are leaving, she takes the opportunity to write. She has received the money order and is moved by Francesca's generosity. There are constant expenses for the clothings and a stream of arrivals and departures. She would like to tell her many things, but it is late and she does not feel very well. She entrusts her to the Lord.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am with you again, though late, but tomorrow the Sisters must leave and so I take the opportunity to write. Listen, how much good this dear widow will do for the hospital! Watch her a little; if not, exchange her. I hope you have received my letter telling you to send Sr. A. Innocenza at once together with Sr. A. Battistina; I am very anxious, I cannot be at peace.2 I am also sending one from Ovada, whom it would be good to put in the house at S. P. d'Arena, because she is very good, in spirit that is, and a goose, but she would be suitable for the house.3

2. I have received your letter with the money order. Ah, dear daughter! I assure you I would have burst into tears, were I not so hard to move to tears, at seeing it sent so quickly and then considering that perhaps you need it yourself. Only today a little came to me,4 but you know what this house is like: there is no end of things to make and continual clothings, in short a perpetual coming and going. What a horror, my God! I assure you it is a factory; but you know it better than I without my telling you.

3. I would like to tell you many things, but what can I do, it is late and I do not feel very well. Every day something new comes upon me.5

M3

4. Goodbye; may my God give you a little sweet, for I am asking Him and

I hope He will not be slow to hear me. Hold fast to Him and love Him, and

you will see that He will give. Yours on earth and in heaven,

affectionately, M.

5. Thank you; for charity's sake do not send me any more vegetables,

because they disagreed with me, nor chocolate, for this year you

[have] sent me a lot; I think I shall have more than one piece; for your

guidance.

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 the two Sisters must leave: the widow (no further details are known),

who may perhaps work well in the hospital; otherwise let her exchange her for an-

other from the Genoa house. My letter: L 345; in para. 1 she said she would

call for Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi.

3 She was also sending a Sister transferred from Ovada, whom she thinks it well to assign

to the community of the Sampierdarena Institute, for household tasks, because she is

of good spirit but not very “quick” intellectually.

4 a few pennies, but quite insufficient for the needs of the house.

5 a new illness.

Answering her questions, she instructs her on how to conduct herself with the Children of Mary and at school. She asks for news of the Cardinal Vicar's visits to the School and enlightens her with spiritual counsel, so that she may advance on the way of the love of God.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am answering the two letters I have received from you since you have been in Rome; they were most welcome.1

2. You want to know how to conduct yourself regarding the Children of Mary, whether you should take Sr. A. Panasia's place. Yes, my daughter, you must do as she did; as for the Congregation, you must not show yourself timid but all on fire for the Congregation of Mary, encouraging the members. Do the same in the schools.2

3. Goodbye; I would like one thing: describe to me properly what the Cardinal Vicar said,3 for I hear he has already come to see you twice; what did he say to you? How pleased he showed himself; in short, you must tell me everything; for charity's sake, when he comes give him the warmest of welcomes; and you, as teacher, ask his blessing, and for the schools too. Show yourself good and docile; in short, the spirit of the Institute must be in your faces, is that not so, my daughter?4

4. So, courage, strength and love of God; think always of Jesus, try to do everything in God's presence and be humble [in] everything, reflecting that whatever good you do will have been done by our dear Master Jesus, who in His infinite goodness deigns to stoop down and do for us what, being such

paltry creatures, we are unable to do at all. Enough, I hope my daughter will be observant of the Rules, the timetable and meditation. St Teresa used to say that whoever does not meditate is not sure of being saved. Yes, in meditation we learn to love, and whoever comes to meditate well is sure to obtain the love of God. Ah, daughter, when you have that, blessed are you, for nothing will remain for you to desire but to grow in it until you are consumed in Him.5 Write to me often and believe me your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Only the first, of 23 October '74, has been preserved in the archive, so

her questions can only be inferred from the Mother's answers.

2 How to conduct herself with the Children of Mary (cf. L 234,16), whom she directed, having

replaced Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi. Not to show herself timid but all on fire,

zealous and a good leader, and at school self-possessed and confident.

3 The Cardinal Vicar Costantino Patrizi.

4 Show yourself: here is the portrait of Irene, one of the first little orphans

taken into the Mother House and raised by her with love. Now, together with the other Sisters,

she is being formed in the spirit of the Institute.

5 So, courage, strength and love of God: these are the guiding lines of

a life intense in prayer and work, under the guidance of the dear Master Jesus

and directed towards attaining the love of God, to the point of being consumed in Him.

She informs her of changes of Sisters still to be made and already made. She confides her fatigue and health problems. She finds comfort in Francesca's filial expressions and conduct.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter and hear that you complain of having no letters from me. Listen, I have so much work that I have not a breath to spare, so weighed down am I; tomorrow Sr. A. Vincenza leaves, today others left; in short, I cannot find the time.1

2. Listen, you tell me you have sent the Sister to Sestri; you did well; it will be good for her to stay there. Look, today I sent them the Parmigiani girl, who wants to become a religious, so she will do her year of training, and so the Sister could study and teach with the girl.2

3. I hear that Sr. A. Enrichetta cannot hold out; so she can stay out of class and just look in from time to time, and then teach Sr. A. Guglielma and the girl in the evening; so they will make progress, and it may be that this Sister gets into the way of it and stays there gladly, and Sr. A. Salvatore would be freed for me, for I would need a Sister of long-standing vocation to send to a house that is to be opened.3

4. Try to pay a visit to Sestri. If you only knew: I sent Sr. A. Carmelina to S. P. d'Arena together with the girl, but I had told them to go to Genoa first; but once she was out, this one said to the Sister: “I am going to S. P. d'Arena”. What heads, my God! See what she will have done. She forgot the Superior's letter; I enclose it, and you will send it on.

5. One would need a thousand heads instead of one as small as mine, which always aches, because I believe my brain is wearing away, for there is a real void there, and I feel the pain comes from its not being full enough; enough, let us leave it all.

6. Your letters are a real comfort to me; your expressions and your good progress comfort me and assure me that I shall have my dear daughter with me for eternity. Yes! you are too dear to me, so you must let me always feel an anxious throb for your good.

7. I commend the house at Sestri to you, and listen to what I have written to the Superior. I want some religious removed from that house at S. P. d'Arena, because they seem too many to me. As for that nun you spoke of at Genoa, you did well; I had not sent her for you at all, I had sent her for Sestri; she is a complete goose.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 tomorrow, 4 November, Sr. A. Vincenza leaves for Terricciola. Other Sisters have left for various destinations.

1 The Sister for Sestri: the one from Cortemaggiore, Sr. A. Guglielma Merli, cf. L 342,3; today I sent the Parmigiani girl (a young teacher) to Sestri, and so the other (Sr. A. Guglielma) could study and teach, helping the Parmigiani girl in class.

3 Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli, the teacher, cannot hold out, stay in

the classroom for health reasons, so she can confine herself to supervising the school and

in the evening give lessons to the girl and to Sr. A. Guglielma; it might be that the lat-

ter would take to it (get into the way of it) and stay gladly at Sestri; then I would transfer Sr.

A. Del Salvatore Orsi.

4 Try to pay some visits to the house at Sestri. I have transferred Sr. A. Car-

melina Carretta to the Sampierdarena Institute; she left with the girl (the Parmi-

giani girl). She forgot the letter of the Superior of Sestri, Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi.

She has decided to send Sr. A. Maddalena for the school, but is keeping her with her for now; meanwhile Carlotta can present the certificate to the Inspector. The Countess has asked for more religious and must be satisfied. She urges prudence regarding the things she has asked for; she should be more precise and send a list of what is needed.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Listen carefully: I am sending you Sr. A. Maddalena, who has promised me to do well and not to vex you; moreover, being very good at her studies, she will make a good showing;2 meanwhile you will go to the Inspector with this certificate and the application I am sending you already filled in,3 and if you do not want to go you can send someone, but it is better that you go; and if he asks about the teacher, tell him she has to finish some affairs of her own and will soon be there; and if by chance he should come, tell him she is at Piacenza on important business; so you will be telling the truth. She is here, but you must know that I want to test her well first, because these teachers have heads that frighten one.

2. So try to do well; the Countess wrote to me that she has sent you a sack of grain and wants me to increase the religious.4 Listen, the one I am sending you is very good, so she will be pleased, and meanwhile she will learn; then, if you have too many, I shall take them away when I send you the teacher; for now she must be satisfied.

3. Listen, when you write to me try not to leave so much blank paper, but write at the top of the page as I do, because it is a fault against poverty.5 Try to manage well regarding the teacher, and

be careful to say nothing about Sr. A. Maddalena not having a certificate; on the contrary, before the schoolgirls and people outside and inside you must let her pass as certified, always without telling a lie. For charity's sake, keep everything well secret from those inside and outside. Do you understand? Be sure to say nothing to anyone.

4. You write to me to send you things; my daughter, you know well

that we have no warehouses here, so you must specify

what you want and how much, of what quality, and for whom it is

intended, and then I shall try to send you what you need.6 Take care

not to give in too much; what is needed, yes, but you know well

that religious are leeches, and it would take far too much to satisfy

all their wishes. Send me a list and I will send you everything. I think

I have made myself clear.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and believe me always your

affectionate M. R.

5. I commend observance to you, and also courage. Cou-

rage; take care of your health and pray, pray, my dear daugh-

ter, for with prayer everything will be obtained,

your affectionate M. R.

1 This letter was included in Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's bundle, but

from its content and context it seems to be to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

2 Having transferred the teacher, cf. L 341, she sends her Sr. A. Maddalena Ter-

zaghi, who, having a fair education (being good at her studies), will be able to

help run the school well.

3 You will go to the Inspector and give him the certificate I am sending (this one) and

the application; should he ask you about the holder of the certificate, you will answer

that she is at Piacenza.

4 Countess Maria Anna Trotti; the one I am sending: Sr. A. Maddalena.

5 not to leave blank paper. Sr. A. Carlotta was in the habit of beginning her

letters a little over halfway down the page. This detail too confirms that she is

the addressee of the letter.

6 In her letter to the Mother of 31 October she had written: “the Sisters would

need dresses, bodices and drawers, so I beg you to provide them”.

She sends him the documents for collecting the dowries of two novices. She gives him news of Sr. A. Vincenza's departure and work.

A.M.F. My Father,

1. Last night I received your letter and hear of the wicked tongues, so zealous!1 I am sending you the papers; I hope you will be able to check them and, God willing, then hand them to Sr. A. Domenica.2

2. Sr. A. Vincenza has left for Terricciola, and I have already had news that she was received with singing and enthusiasm; from there she goes to S. Martinello for the 20th of this month, and I hope that for the Immaculate Conception she will be two days at Foligno. I would like to tell you many more things, but I am alone and have an abyss of writing to do.

I am your

humble, devoted Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The wicked tongues: “Monsignor (Negrotto), on his way to the Parrocchietta,

told me that those (Sisters) at the Fornaci suffer even in their food, and the ones

with so much charity are, as usual, the Parish Priest and that Fr Giuseppe, who tell

Monsignor all the tittle-tattle”, so Fr Donadio on 5 November.

2 The papers: the documents he had been seeing to for collecting the dowry of two

Sisters. (Cf. L 338, n. 1). He can collect the money and hand it to the Superior

Domenica Marchesini, Superior at the Fornaci.

She blesses the Lord on hearing that Vincenza is at Terricciola and urges her to look after herself and not tire herself out. She should go to the Bishop now that she has time.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am answering your last letter in haste; I am glad to hear you have reached Terricciola; God be blessed for it.1 For charity's sake, take care of yourself. I am sorry to hear you have stomach pains; mind, it is a bad sign; look after yourself, do not overdo it, for charity's sake.

2. I am well, and so is everyone; try to send me postulants, for I need them, soon.2 It is Saturday and we have no end of work. Goodbye; do not be upset if I write little, but time is too short.

Goodbye,

your affectionate M.

3. I fear you may have made a mistake in taking the Rules,

and that instead of taking the common ones you took those for con-

fessors.3 If so, write to me at once and I will send them to you. It would be well

for you, while you have nothing to do, to take the opportunity to go to the Bishop;4 so

you will receive a blessing for me, and thank him for the Pope's

blessing.

Goodbye; greet the Sisters for me.

1 your last, of 5 November.

2 try to send me postulants. “The archpriest is a man all

zeal and love for his people; he is always in the confessional, every morning there are almost fifty communions, nearly all Children of Mary, whom he looks after so well”... so Vincenza had written to her. The field is therefore well cultivated, and the Mother sees it as fruitful in vocations for the Institute.

3 instead of the fundamental Rules; the others contained norms reserved

for confessors.

4 while you have nothing to do: Sr. A. Vincenza had written to her: “we are still in the

archpriest's house because in ours there is not yet a free room; the

windows are missing, everything is cluttered with masons”; take the opportunity to go to the Bish-

op (Mgr Ferdinando Capponi, Bishop of Volterra), the Mother suggests. (Cf.

L 359, n. 1). Sr. A. Vincenza went there on 10 November accompanied by the Archpriest

Secondo Griselli.

Various counsels on how to conduct herself in running the community. She asks for prayers for a good outcome of the dispute with the Ricchini brothers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you a couple of lines in reply for Sr. A. Perpetua's sister; read them to her, then have her write the address; send it to its destination.

2. I hear from your letter, which I received this morning, what Sr. A. Gerolama is doing. Listen, where Fr Accinelli is concerned you can let him act; you know he does everything for the good of the house; let her go to confession;1 and I am also very glad that those at Invorio are settling down; I am truly pleased.2

3. I commend the school to you; I hope soon to send you the printed book;3 and I am glad to hear that providence always comes to you.

4. Have some prayers said to Saint Anne to free me from taking the oaths. Also have special prayers said in common every day to Our Lady of the Heart of Jesus; there is the appropriate prayer, as you know. For charity's sake, let them pray to this dear Virgin that I may be freed from such oaths. The sentence is coming soon; pray, pray, God can do all things. Ah, yes! May He convert these two unhappy priests once and for all.4

Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Gerolama Piralli had asked Fr Accinelli to write to her 644

relatives about financial matters concerning her. (L Fr Accinelli to M. Rosa, 18.10.74).

2 The postulants of Invorio, who had received the habit of the Daughters of Saint

Anne, were being formed for religious life.

3 The school: practical lessons for the nurses, generally given, where pos-

sible, every day by the Superiors, using a manual prepared for the Daughters of

Saint Anne.

4 This is the Ricchini lawsuit, pursued not only by Angelo but also

by his brother Paolo. Cf. L 345, n. 6.

Apologizing for not being able to come in person, she asks his advice on how to proceed in the Ricchini case, as she is being called on to take oaths.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Being unable to come myself and humble myself at Your feet to seek advice on a most important matter, I must make use of the pen, sure that by this means too I shall have the same answer from Your immense charity, of which I have had no few proofs.

2. Your Excellency well knows that the Work of Saint Anne is involved in a lawsuit,3 and after it has been won several times, now, the opponent finding no other means, oaths are imposed on me: either swear or return the money he gave me to set up a house seven years ago,4 which still exists, full of girls and nuns, many of the girls having been placed there by the said priest and kept free of charge. Now I wish to know how I should proceed.

3. Having only a few days in which to reply, I beg Your Excellency, for pity's sake, not to leave me without the answer I await before taking any decision. Grant me Your Pastoral Blessing; may it sustain me in such adversity.

[Most humble Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO]

1 In the autograph draft (MaM-10) the addressee is missing; it is deduced from the

content.

2 The date is deduced from the context. Cf. L 355,2; 357,4.

3 The Archbishop was very well informed. She herself had written to him on another

occasion, cf. L 141.

4 The house had been opened on 14 November 1868.

She returns the proxies to him. She hopes he can collect the money and buy crucifixes for the novices who have none. He is to have prayers said, as she is agitated about the oaths in the case with Fr Ricchini. She has accepted proposals to open houses at Mercatello, Mercatino, Ancona and Lugo. Sr. A. Vincenza is at Terricciola and will then be at Perugia.

A.M.F.

My Father,

1. I am sending you the two papers; who knows whether they will still be in order. Enough; if by good fortune the time has come for you to collect the money, buy me with fifty of it as many crucifixes as usual for the religious, for I have now clothed a good number,1 but they have no crucifix and keep asking me whether Father Agostino has written and is sending them, because I told them I would write to you to obtain them; but first I wanted to hear whether you were collecting these religious' money.

2. My Father, in a few days they are to hear the Ricchini case;2 have some prayers said to St Francis that he may go with his staff. What a weight of pain I carry! You cannot believe it; I feel a constant agitation at the thought of the oaths. Perhaps they will hear it in 10 or 15 days; tell the Sisters to pray, and all the good souls you know.

4. I have settled three more houses: one at Mercatello, another at Mercatino, and also at Ancona, about which the Cardinal wrote me a most beautiful letter; and I have also settled Lugo.3

5. You will know that Sr. A. Vincenza is at Terricciola, and by the twentieth

she will be at Perugia.4 If she does not arrive in time for the date I have fixed for these other houses, then I shall go myself. The one at Mercatello is in the diocese of Pesaro, and I go there gladly because it is a good municipality, the negotiations having been conducted together with the Curia. I will not speak to you of my health, because I can tell you nothing good; I am very poorly, especially my head.

Your poorest Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 I am sending you: cf. L 351, n. 2. Who knows whether the documents will still be valid; but

if he collects the money, let him spend 50 F of it on the usual crucifixes for the religious, of whom I have

clothed a good number...

2 The Ricchini case: cf. L 354. Tell the Sisters to pray. She too has asked

and keeps asking for special prayers, cf. L 353,4; 345, n. 6; 357,4. L 376,4.

3 Mercatello, cf. L 356; Mercatino Conca (L 374); Ancona, L 336,1; Lugo di

Ravenna, L 346.

4 She had told him so on 7 November (cf. L 351,2).

She is glad to learn of the Town Council's favourable decision about the Sisters' coming. She draws his attention to certain points: the addition of a fourth Sister and premises with the bare essentials, and asks for the date the Sisters are to arrive.

[Reverend Archpriest],

1. I am replying to your most esteemed letter, which I have the pleasure of receiving today, the 12th of this month. I am delighted to hear that the Most Honourable Council welcomed my letter and that all is in order to arrange our arrival.

2. Now allow me first to make an observation that seems to me most just and which Your Most Reverend Lordship will doubtless accept. Since the three Sisters will be continually occupied in the three schools,1 a fourth seems to me altogether necessary, to prepare a little food for them and do whatever is needed in their small dwelling, as we have no maidservants, nor may we keep any.

3. Do not trouble yourself too much about our dwelling, since we are accustomed to make do with bare necessities, such as a table for meals, the necessary chairs, a wardrobe for the linen and a writing table. As for the premises, if the rooms are large enough for three or four to sleep in, the beds must have curtains; a small room for receiving visitors, with chairs only; one for meals; the kitchen with the necessary utensils, and household linen that is plain, yes, but new.

4. I would like you to indicate roughly when – if you decide to proceed – I should send them, as I also have another house to open in this neighbourhood.2 I forgot to tell you that the journey must be at your expense. In the sweet hope that the poor Daughters

of Saint Anne may lend their Work in your Municipality, please bless me, as I have the honour to sign myself Your Reverend Lordship's

most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 the three Sisters continually occupied in the three schools: engaged con-

tinually in the three classes...

2 another in the neighbourhood: at Mercatino Conca, also in the province of Urbino,

like Mercatello.

She is worried by Vincenza's silence. Everything is going on in order, with perfect observance in her way of life. She has accepted a house at Mercatello and another at Mercatino. She asks for fervent prayers for the “Ricchini lawsuit”.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to you first, as soon as I sit down at the desk;1 I have had no letters from you for two days, and it makes me anxious; I fear for your health; I assure you it weighs heavily on me; for charity's sake, take care of yourself.

2. In my examination last night I found that it did not at all please the Lord that both you and Sr. A. Francesca kept up a way of life with me such as lingering in the evening;2 you cannot believe how much more observant I am now that I do not linger at all, and so I keep silence all day; in the evening, when the rosary is over, I shut myself in my room. If I have writing to do I stay in the study, but alone, in silence; and in the morning I do what I can to get up early.
