3. Everything is going on in order; I have accepted another house at Urbino, that is, via Urbino for Mercatello, and another at Mercatino; who knows whether it may not come to join you.3

4. Listen, have some prayers said for the lawsuit; it will be heard in a few days, and your uncle replied to you saying that I shall certainly have to take the oaths, but God can do all things, and prayer moves mountains. For charity's sake, commend me to the good young religious, and I promise you a month of communions for this grace;

form the intention well; I am writing everywhere asking for prayers. Ah, my God, what pain!4

5. You will have received my letter; the post has just come and there are no letters from you; for charity's sake, do what you can. I add nothing more, because I have so much work. Goodbye,

your affectionate M.

God bless you, and believe me yours for all ages.

1 A line to you first: before anyone else, as soon as I sat down at the desk to write.

2 In reviewing her life before the Lord she found, the previous

evening, that He is not pleased with Francesca and Vincenza's settled habit of

staying on in the evening to talk with her... Now I am much more observant of the strict

silence prescribed by the Rule.

3 If both places call soon, it is possible that she will go herself and

join her.

4 Cf. L 355, n. 2.

She knows the cause of Carlotta's illness and so invites her to come to her. She expects her at once, grieved to know she is suffering. She herself cannot move because of her work and poor health. She awaits her. Let her promise Jesus that she will obey, set out, unburden herself to her Mother and be consoled by her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I understand where your illness comes from; listen, you would give me a great present if you could come over here to me; I have so many things to tell you, lovely ones, not ugly, which will be a real consolation to you; and meanwhile you will take the teacher and bring me the Sister.1

2. Come, my dear daughter, leaning on obedience; come, and you will be completely cured and able to take up your work again for the glory of God and the good of your neighbour. I expect you at once; do not delay; I will give you the money for the journey; I am waiting for you. Carlotta, all mine for eternity, you certainly do not know how dear you are to me, and hearing that you are ill grieves me too much.2 Had I not seen a few lines of yours on the back of one from Sr. A. Maddalena, I would have come at once.3

3. My dear daughter, if you only knew how worn out I am with work! Sr. A. Vincenza is away, so I have the whole burden of the desk and the letters; I always have a bad headache, and besides we have so many houses to open, so I must prepare the Sisters.4

4. Goodbye, I am waiting for you. Say to dear Jesus: “I want to obey and I want to go to my Mother and unburden myself; meanwhile she will console me”. Leave Sr. A. Costantina as

Superior, that is, in your place for 24 hours. Tell them to say nothing, because nothing can happen in twenty-four hours. Yours for all ages,

affectionately, MOTHER R.

1 I understand where your illness comes from. Having received no letters from the Mo-

ther she had lost heart: “I want to know whether you are displeased with me... and whether you

still regard me as your daughter, because from this silence I foresee that there is something

wrong”, so on 12.11.74.

2 The Mother finds the healing remedy at once: come... leaning on obe-

dience (because she felt ill)... I expect you at once. So she calms her fears even be-

fore embracing and consoling her. Feeling ill: Carlotta had written to her:

“God knows why He keeps me so oppressed and pierced”.

3 Had I not had the letter in your own hand after the one from Sr. A.

Maddalena, I would have come to you.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza is away; we have houses to open. Cf. L 355,4-5.

She tells her the day on which the Sisters are to meet her at Florence station to go to Perugia. Vincenza will then go to Foligno. She suggests what to write to her uncle about their work and the “Ricchini lawsuit”.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter and hear how well you were received by the good bishop.1 My God, when our Superiors receive us well, everything is blessed by God!

2. I hope to send the Superior to Foligno on Monday or Wednesday, and then you can write, both to me and to the Superior Sr. A. Eufemia, the time and day when we are to meet, that is, the Sisters; I must have them be at Florence and Sr. A. Eufemia must go to Perugia, do you understand?2 I would be of the opinion that it should be Thursday the 19th of this month, since the twentieth falls on a Friday and you have no time to stay; just two days will be too few.

3. Perhaps Sr. A. Eufemia will be accompanied by Signora Maria, who will then do very well for your return journey to Foligno, for I long for you to go there;3 meanwhile do not forget, at Foligno, that money: have notice given, lest the term expire and it can no longer be drawn. I hope you took the two hundred francs and a little more.4 Have Mancini's postulants never arrived?5

4. How much work there is at this desk! Today my hand hurt so much that I had to rub it with that water in order to go on.6 How dear your letters were to me!

5. Listen, write a little to your uncle; thank him for the letter he

wrote you and tell him you are travelling about setting up houses, and tell him the number 26, as is true, since they have been settled; that we shall certainly meet at Lugo or Pesaro; you can tell him we are one here and one there, so great is the crowd of requests; and this only so that it may be of use to him for the hearing in a few days' time; today the two lawyers met to prepare.7 Write to him at once and tell him always to address his letters to you at Piacenza, and that you will be very glad if he keeps you informed.

6. So we are agreed that on Thursday the 19th of this month I shall have the religious leave at 11 at night, so as to be at Florence at half past 7 in the morning.8

Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and all of them; your

affectionate M. R.

1 The letter is of 11 November and speaks at length of the welcome from the

Bishop of Volterra, Mgr Ferdinando Capponi.

2 when we are to meet, or rather, the Sisters are to meet at Florence

and Sr. A. Eufemia Camporesi is to go to Perugia.

3 Perhaps she will be accompanied by Signora Maria Grampini, who can

keep you company on your journey to Foligno.

4 I hope you took, brought with you, the 200 F. They had been given by the father

of a postulant from Peccioli, Vincenza had written to her.

5 Fr Mancini: cf. L 315,8. He had already presented several postulants.

6 my hand hurt: cf. L 316, n. 5.

7 The uncle, the lawyer Domenico Boccardo, was defending the Mother in the Ricchini case.

Tell him that our houses number 26 (the number 26), as is true, since agreements have already

been made for other foundations; and that we shall certainly meet (join up) at

Lugo and Pesaro; ...so great is the number (the crowd) of requests; you will say this only

so that it may be of use to him for the defence, that is, as proof of the soundness of the Institute

to be presented in court. Today the two lawyers

(Boccardo and Debernardis) met to prepare and agree.

8 At 7.30.

This letter will be handed to her by the teacher, an excellent creature, who replaces the other Sister, whom she is to send away. She advises her how to deal with a lady who wants to meddle in the affairs of the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive this letter from the teacher; she will run the school; I commend her to you; you understand me, she likes to be made a little fuss of;2 leave the other two who are there, and the other one who is with them put with the boarders, and remove Luigia at once, for I am uneasy since she told me she knows so many ugly things. Meanwhile, this one is very good and you will be very pleased; and at the first opportunity send Luigia here; meanwhile keep an eye on her and forbid her to talk with the others, and especially with these new ones.3

2. How is providence? and your health? This teacher will be a great relief to you, and you will be able to take counsel with her. For charity's sake, try with your good way of acting — I hope you will see to it that she becomes wholly Saint Anne's.4 Goodbye, your

affectionate [MOTHER]

3. Write and tell me you are well. Listen, go with her to the Inspector to put yourselves in order.5

4. You write that Signora Maria has written you certain things that upset you.6 Despise it all; we are not obliged to answer anonymous letters; it means they are people who cannot

show their faces. So take no notice; if she should write again and put her address, then answer her in black ink, saying that you beg her to remain the lay person she is and not to meddle in things that do not concern her, since you have your superiors and are in no way bound to receive corrections from her. Let her beware of doing so, being a poor lay woman who does not know what religion means.7 I hope she will not write such things to you again. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. R.

1 This letter, though dated, was included in the undated bundle of Sr. A.

Vincenza Rapallino. It is clearly addressed to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

2 from the teacher. This is Sr. A. Onorata Casati; she likes to be treated affection-

ately (made a fuss of).

3 You will transfer (remove) Sr. A. Luigia, because she knows of things that might

circulate among the Sisters and give scandal, especially to the newcomers.

4 wholly Saint Anne's. Sr. A. Onorata had received the religious habit on 29 Sep-

tember 1874, so she was to be formed in the spirit of the Institute.

5 with her... in order. Present the young woman and the necessary do-

cuments to the school Inspector for authorization to teach.

6 In her letter (of 14.11.74) Sr. A. Carlotta had written to her: “I receive a letter

from Signora Maria, who reproaches me a great deal and among other things tells me to

be kind and treat the Sisters and pupils with love... she has written me an

anonymous letter”.

7 To remain a lay person: to act, that is, as an outsider and not meddle in

things that do not concern her. She does not know, cannot understand, the spirit that animates

religious life.

She has had a letter from the Marchioness Spinola, who has promised to give the subsidy for this month. Vincenza is to ask her to give her opinion of the Religious. The Mother has written to the Duchess proposing to close the elementary school and keep only home nursing and, if needed, the sewing school for the older girls. Vincenza should therefore see what is to be done. But she must insist that catechism be taught in church every Sunday and enclosure be observed, with outsiders not allowed into the Sisters' rooms.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. You will receive this letter from the hands of Sr. A. Eufemia. First of all, the Marchioness has written to me saying that as soon as you arrive she will give you fr. 50 for November, although the month is already well advanced, and that for the rest you will find everything ready; so she tells me.2 Tell her that if she is not satisfied with any of the religious she should write to me and we will make a change at once; and likewise, if anything is not to her liking, she should tell me frankly, for I will try to satisfy her in everything.

2. Meanwhile listen: I am writing to Signora Maria to try to accompany Sr. A. Eufemia to Perugia, and then she would serve for your return; enough; I feel clearly, as I write, that this weighs on you and you do not like it; so I hope in the Lord that Sr. A. Eufemia will manage well and travel by day, and so nothing will happen.3 Meanwhile, for charity's sake, write to me as soon as you arrive.

3. When you go to Foligno, look into things; first of all write to the Inspector that Sr. A. Carmelina is no longer at Foligno and had to leave for reasons of health, and tell him that if the schools continue another teacher will be provided,4 because you must know that I have written to the Duchess that I would be inclined to give up the academic school altogether and keep, if any want to come, the older girls for sewing, and for the rest have nurses as at Genoa, which seems to me much better, and it is also clear that this work is far dearer to the town than the schools; and besides, you can understand that I do not know how to manage, having so many houses to open.5 Ah, if it could be arranged, how good it would be to achieve this!

4. Listen, I heard from Sr. A. Eufemia that catechism was no longer even being taught in church; be sure to tell Sr. A. Giovannina never to give it up; you will see to it.6

5. How dreadful! I hear that all the secular priests went into the sick Sisters' room, even the D...'s maids. Find out more and put things in order. Signora Maria will have to be allowed in, for I hear it would cause too much of a stir, as she is a benefactress and has grown used to it. See to it all properly, and let the two sick Sisters be together.7

6. Dear daughter, how dreadful! The bills for the clothings: one is a thousand 149 and the other 900; what do you say? I have paid the smith, and it was 79. In short, there is nothing else to be done, my God! See that you can be sure of collecting Tuzzi's money;8 at S. Martinello get things done quickly, so that you can stay a little longer at Foligno.

Goodbye, all [yours] for all ages,

affectionately, M.

1 The date is deduced from the fact that it was handed to her by Sr. A. Eufemia

Camporesi, the new Superior, who was to meet Sr. A. Vincenza on

20.11 (cf. L 359,6).

2 The Marchioness Edvige Spinola.

3 Signora Maria Grampini (cf. L 359, n. 3). I feel that it displeases you (weighs on you)

to have to travel with her, so I hope Sr. A. Eufemia can leave by day.

4 At Foligno she will have to decide about the school. First she will inform the school

Inspector of Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta's departure and her replacement, if

the school continues to operate.

5 She will also study with the Duchess Agnese di Sora – already informed by the Mother by

letter – the scaling down of the Daughters of Saint Anne's activities at Foligno. The

Mother thinks it advisable to close the school, also because she does not have many certified teachers and must meet the needs of the new houses.

6 She must also restore the teaching of catechism in the Parish,

urging Sr. Giovannina Pizzorno to take responsibility for it.

7 Outsiders went into the room of the two sick Sisters, priests

and even the Duchess's maids. Enclosure must be observed. An exception

will have to be made for Signora Maria Grampini.

8 Tuzzi's money: Sr. A. Biagia, of Foligno, was to receive part of

her dowry in cash.

She urges them not to worry about the Superior: there is nothing serious, she no longer has a fever and will soon be back among them. Meanwhile let them be prudent, obedient and silent, and pray a great deal.

A.M.F.

My daughters,

1. I heard from Sr. A. Benedetta how troubled you all are about your Superior.1 Be at peace, for it is nothing; it was all gossip and misunderstandings and nothing more, permitted by God, who wishes to test us in this way; but courage.

2. Let us learn from Peter, the Saviour's successor, not to flee from sorrows but to work courageously in the way of the Lord.2

3. I want you to say nothing more about it among yourselves; rumours spread, and the tongue is a knife that cuts with seven blades.3 For charity's sake, silence; in a few days your Superior will be with you, I mean the Superior Sr. A. Carlotta. Since yesterday she has had no fever and is beginning to improve; so be at peace, and pray much to the good God for me.

4. I want all your conversation to be holy, and your actions too. Obey; I shall soon be with you. Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and believe me always your poor

M. ROSA

1 She has heard from Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega that they are worried about the Supe-

rior. Accepting the Mother's invitation (cf. L 358,2), she had gone to Piacen-

za to be with her.

2 Let us learn from Peter to follow the Saviour and work with courage

(Mt 5:18-19).

3 I want you not to speak of it, because the tongue can do so much harm.

“If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue... his religion

is vain” (Jas 1:26).

She will send him the two certificates. For the opening of the Hospital she will provide a Superior skilled in surgery and dentistry.

[Reverend Archpriest]

1. I thank you infinitely for your most esteemed letter, which I have the honour of receiving today, the 19th of this month. How obliged I am to you for the trouble you took on our behalf in preference to other, better Institutes! Everything is settled; within eight days Your Reverend Lordship will have the two certificates.1

2. As Superior I intend to send you a capable one, also for the opening of the hospital,2 already experienced, who will be able at once, if you so wish, to put that charity into practice, since in the hospital where she is now an assistant she is accustomed to the school of surgery, having also the duty of extracting teeth. I will try to provide her with her instruments,3 so that she can be of use to poor humanity.

With a thousand respects to the Honourable Council, and begging Your Most Reverend Lordship to bless me, I remain with all esteem and veneration

your most humble and devoted Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The letter is of 16 November. Everything is settled: as to the number

of Sisters, four not three (cf. L 356,2), and the annual payment for each

(L 350), as proposed to her.

2 also for the opening of the hospital: the new community was to take on,

besides the girls' school, the management of the small hospital. (Cf. L of Fra Paci-

fico Sampaolesi, 9 November 1874, AFSA, FcIC).

3 with her necessary instruments.

She has learnt that Francesca is ill and is greatly distressed at the thought that she herself was the cause, having sent her to the station on foot. She will have prayers said for her. She need not worry about Sr. A. Carlotta, who is content and steadfast.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter, my Francesca, wholly mine,

1. For pity's sake take care of yourself; ah, do not kill me; hearing that you are ill pains me more than everything else.1 God will see to it; the Sisters have arrived, and I knew it only now, at 8 in the morning.2 I was anxious all night, because I kept thinking of you being ill.

2. Today a triduum to the Eternal Father begins for your recovery. Alas, I feel my heart is breaking, my Francesca; I made a great mistake, which cost me tears at the thought that I sent you to the station on foot. Oh, how dreadful, and you will have suffered.3 Ah, forgive me, for pity's sake! Perhaps it was this that caused the bleeding.4 So take care of yourself.

3. You tell me to send her things.5 Never; everything has been settled. Sr. A. Carlotta remains steadfast and content; those who came to fetch her have already left, satisfied.6 For the rest, I shall write to you at greater length.

4. This evening I am [sending this] so that it reaches you. Rest easy, everything is settled and in order. The battles are calming down. Go ahead according to your judgement, without waiting for orders from me. Do what God inspires you to do, and I approve and bless it all.

Yours affectionately for all ages,

M. R.

1 take care of yourself... everything else. Her poor health pains her more

than the unpleasant events in the Sampierdarena community: the flight of the Supe-

rior Augusta and of Sr. A. Tecla Mazzini, and the resulting unrest in the community.

Sr. A. Francesca had had to hurry there to assess the situation and

apply the remedies needed for good order. She had therefore had to talk, clarify,

calm things down and send some Sisters to Piacenza.

2 The transferred Sisters had arrived in the evening.

3 I sent you to the station. She had asked her to accompany the Sis-

ters mentioned above to the station in person.

4 This must have caused the haemoptysis.

5 To send Sr. A. Augusta's things.

6 Sr. A. Carlotta (Augusta's sister) is steadfast; the family members who

had gone to persuade her to go with them for treatment had left

satisfied.

She denounces the grave injustice of the discriminatory pay between the resident girls and the outside workers and gives notice that she will withdraw hers unless it is remedied.

Most Illustrious Signor Emilio Poss,

1. It grieves me greatly to have to tell you that I cannot continue to leave some 70 girls working in your factory for such low wages, while the outside workers receive eighty centesimi each and we the wretched sum of 20 or 25 centesimi, and one or two forty.1

2. Consider that if at the end of the month, the first of December, if at the end or the beginning of that month I do not have an increase, I am resolved to withdraw them.2

Please accept my sentiments of respect and esteem.

Your most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 the outside workers were paid more; they were put for-

ward and therefore protected by the Prefecture of Piacenza.

2 Consider. She is precise and peremptory. She means: if the increase is not

paid in advance, on 1 December or at the end of that month, she will withdraw the

girls.

She did not write sooner because she was waiting for the teacher to leave so as to send what Carlotta had asked for; that is the only reason, not that she does not love her. She warns her about a Sister's way of behaving towards Superiors. Other instructions and news.

My daughter,

1. I have just finished reading your two lines and am answering at once, though my head is bandaged because of the pain. What a comfort it was to hear you are better! You complain that I do not write to you. My dear, you know, the reason is this: every day I thought I would be able to tell you the teacher was coming; and my affection for my dear daughter is too great. Who put such ugly thoughts into your head? For charity's sake, never let it be so!

2. Listen, I forgot to tell you to be careful not to let yourself be ensnared by the Sister I sent you,2 because she has always done so with all her Superiors and is very insincere. For charity's sake, watch her and keep her in her place like the others.

3. Listen, the religious teacher I have is not suitable for Ferrara and I am obliged to send you a lay one.3 I hear what you say about the Sister; very well, look, I shall withdraw her; you know well that journeys cost money, and this year they are no small expense for me.4 Enough; if Sr. A. Rosa can no longer stay there, you can get me a doctor's certificate like the other you sent me, and then I can tell the Countess that I withdrew her on the doctor's orders.5

4. Then they can come together, and next Wednesday I shall send you the teacher, and you will send back to me, with those who are to come, the certificate I sent you, and renew the application in the name of the one who will arrive.

5. For the rest, the caps, drawers and bodices are already prepared; only I am surprised that Sr. A. Maddalena is still looking for things, when she has taken more than her due, and moreover she knows the rules: that she is not to know whether she has three [or] four, but it is enough that on Saturday she always has whatever she needs. Keep her in check, for charity's sake.6

6. Dear daughter, take care of yourself, and when you have more means, or at least no debts, you can slip away into my arms; I await you and remain

your affectionate M. R... God bless you, and I am your M...

1 This letter was classified among those addressed to Sr. A. Vincenza Ra-

pallino; it is instead to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini: cf. L 350, n. 1.

2 not to let yourself be ensnared, cunningly won over, by the Sister I

sent you (perhaps Sr. A. Maddalena, cf. L 350,1).

3 a lay one: a lay teacher.

4 I hear what you say: In the letter of 19.11 that she is answering, Carlotta had written: “Sr.

A. Onorata is cold and knows nothing... she is sad and says one cannot live here”.

The Mother is of a mind to withdraw her.

5 if Sr. A. Rosa can no longer stay. M. Rosa had already decided on her transfer,

but had had to give way because of the opposition of Countess Maria Anna

Trotti. (Cf. L 319,3).

6 The things she has prepared had been asked for by the Superior: cf. L 350,

n. 6. But she warns her against the demands of Sr. A. Maddalena, who has le-

arnt the Institute's customs and knows well that she is not supposed to know how many pieces of

linen she has, and must be content to be given what she normally

needs; keep her in her place, for charity's sake.

She is deeply distressed to hear that Francesca is ill and begs her to take care of herself. As soon as she is well she is to take eight days' leave and come to Piacenza. She need not worry about the Sister, who seems to her repentant. She is to send what remains of the other two's belongings.

A.M.F.

My daughter, dear for all ages,

1. Ah, the pain of hearing you are ill [is great]! I am telegraphing you now; everyone tells me not to, that there will be letters today. For pity's sake have someone write to me; do not exert yourself, stay resting in bed, do not worry; in short, whatever is needed, spare nothing. As soon as you are well, take a little leave for 8 days, and so come and rest a while and be with me.2

2. Do not think any more about those unhappy women, for I already see them very repentant.3 Sr. A. Carmelina weeps and despairs because I have pronounced sentence on her; she sends word, and told me herself, that I should give her whatever penance I like, that she is ready to do it, and that what she did to me was serious. She says not everything Fr Accinelli said is true; in short, it was the devil who made her do it.4 There you are: when they no longer know what to say, they say it was the devil, when they know a trick more than he does. Horrible infamy! Can more be said? To kiss Jesus and then betray him!

3. Oh, dear daughter, how much good this meditation on Judas does me! [When] I am upset and cannot find much recollection, I turn at once to this point, and I assure you that I soon feel so united with my God in sorrow that I cannot help weeping.

4. Tell the Superior to send me the things, all that is left of those two unhappy women, and also those of Sr. A. Pastore, you know, for she needs changing often.5

Goodbye, for I have too much work. Sr. A. Carlotta sends you warm greetings and longs for you as I do; so we shall tell you many more things in person;6 but no one can be as fond of you as I am; but eternally yours,

M. R.

The date has been completed from the context.

2 Cf. L 364,1-2.

the two unhappy women: Augusta Biagini and Tecla Mazzini, who had left the Sampierdarena Institute without permission, taking money and gold objects with them. (Cf. L 364, n. 1).

4 Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta knew of the two unhappy women's

intentions; not only that, she had told Fr Accinelli she wanted “to leave the convent”.

(L Accinelli to M. Rosa, 18.11.74). Now she is at Piacenza, weeping and despairing.

5 Tell the Superior who has replaced Augusta, Sr. A. Elisabetta Veronesi,

to send me what remains of those unhappy women's things and those of Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore

Dosi, because she needs them, being ill.

6 Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

?EH

As the agreements for opening the work have been concluded by both parties, she awaits notice of the date the Sisters are to arrive.

Most Illustrious Congregation,

1. Having received your most esteemed letter requesting four Sisters for the Schools under your direction, and after negotiation the stipend of 1,200 francs having been agreed, together with premises entirely free of any other person: these conditions having been accepted by both parties, the matter is concluded upon your letter of reply informing me when the Sisters are to go there.1

I sign myself

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 382.

She tells her of the arrival of the postulant teacher and asks her to speak to the Superior about her and commend her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Two lines in haste to tell you that tomorrow, by the 4 p.m. train, the teacher for the house1 arrives and will come to the hospital; so have her accompanied. I like her very much; she is with her mamma and will stay until Sunday, or rather Monday, and then she will come back here alone.

2. For charity's sake take care of yourself, and soon, that is, we shall see each other; I long for it. Ask the Superior to treat her with consideration and put her in the refectory with them. Let the food be the same, good as it should be for all. For her, two things: a little wine; I hope Sr. A. Elisabetta2 will grow fond of her, and she will be a great boon to the house. She is very shy; her shyness needs to be helped to pass a little.3 Goodbye, I want to post this,

your affectionate M. I shall write to you again by means of her.4

1 the teacher for the house arrives, for the Institute. She is presumed to be the postulant,

because she asks that she be given her meals in the refectory with the Sisters.

2 Sr. Elisabetta is the Superior.

3 She is very shy; she needs to become self-assured (to have her shy-

ness pass).

4 She will send her a letter by means of the young woman mentioned above. It is L 371.

She tells her of the teacher's arrival and entrusts her to her. She advises her to put the house back on its feet, paying the debts and treating the Sisters well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the teacher and hope she will do well; she is very good and has a splendid certificate; keep an eye on her, and give her the same food as yourselves, a good milky coffee, and you can put her in your refectory; she is no trouble at all.1

2. I have received your letter; it was very dear to me. Yes, my daughter, wretched creatures, who knows where they will end up; I do not know.2 Let us pray for them, that God may give them the grace of perseverance in their vocation.

3. Listen, for charity's sake, watch those two vipers you have in this house carefully, lest they too start scheming; what thieving, my God!3

4. I hear about the bills they have left; it is horrifying; see, for charity's sake, whether you can pay some off with the boarding fees; I also urge you to see that the fees cover bread, maize and pasta, as we had calculated.4

5. I will say no more, for I know how capable you are at economy; so let the religious eat and drink, but not have to suffer any more; the resourceful woman manages everything, with work, with begging.5 Enough, I hope I shall have consolations and see that poor house flourish again. I am sure of it. Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and believe me always your affectionate

M. R.

1 Cf. L 369,2.

2 wretched creatures. The two Sisters who fled from the House. Cf. L 367, n. 3.

3 those two vipers: so the two Vernengo sisters were called. Cf. L 206,

n. 5; che ladronissi is Genoese: latronizzii = thefts.

4 I hear of the debts left by the two mentioned above, n. 2. If you could

pay them off with the girls' fees, and also buy bread, maize and

pasta as we had calculated.

5 begging was one of the means of support.

She is always taken up with many things and has had to stand up to certain people. The enemy is at work, but she hopes soon to see him put to shame. Francesca is to encourage Sr. A. Elisabetta to be a strong woman and not run up large debts.

A.M.F. My Francesca,

1. Today I wrote to tell you the teacher would arrive. She brings you this letter;1 it is odd that I wrote to you and then did not notice that I was speaking to the Superior of the house, telling her what she had to do when this young woman arrived, and how she was to treat her. What will you have said?2

2. You see, there are so many things of such a kind that I must deal with that I really do not know which way to turn to fulfil my obligations; dear Francesca, I hope the moment will soon come when I can talk to you.

3. Oh, how much I have to tell you! Today I had a long battle with Ci in... and Maddalena. I have also broken with Bologna;3 in short, Cifone is putting on a show behind my back, but I hope to break his horns soon and see him roasting under a pot. Enough. Dagger thrusts from every side, but I hope they will rebound on his Cifo.4

4. Encourage Sr. A. Elisabetta; tell her to be a strong and invincible woman, fearing no one, strong.5 I commend the accounts to you: let her not run up large ones. What a martyrdom it is at the moment, under so many expenses! Goodbye (your); greet the Sisters for me.

God bless them, and you in particular, as I am yours for eternity.

Affectionately and closely, M. R.

1 This letter: she had announced it in L 269.

2 I was speaking to the Superior of the house: some of the instructions did not in fact

concern Francesca directly.

3 long battle with Ci in... and Maddalena. Presumably Canon Insani

and Maddalena Parmigiani, over the Cortemaggiore house. As to Bologna,

that is, Countess Trotti, cf. L 373,1.

4 Cifone: a derogatory name, horrid face, cifo, ugly snout. She expresses

a firm will to oppose evil in whatever form it appears.

5 Sr. Elisabetta, the Superior who must repair the damage done by the one who

preceded her.

She advises her to provide the Sisters with overcoats and the clothing they need against the cold. She is to be diligent in requiring reports on the care of the sick and prudent about what comes to her knowledge. She must watch carefully over everything.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received all your letters and the last, in which you told me you are putting something aside. I would like you also to think of clothing the religious and having an overcoat made for each, because I see it is very necessary and they should all have one; likewise drawers and woollen bodices, which protect them well against catching aches, stitches and coughs. I hope you will do it in the same way you did the mattresses.1

2. I also want you to be more diligent in receiving the reports, not to trust to sending the same two Sisters together too often, and to be prudent and not reveal the Sister who has told you of her companion's fault.2

3. I do not know why, but for two days I have had a great fear about the Genoa house; I fear there may be some disorder; in short, watch night and day if you want to do what God commands you through your Superiors.

4. Try to go and visit the sick whom the Sisters are nursing.3

5. As for that gentleman who wants to know about Sr. A. Vincenza and the climate, I do not know what to tell him, because I know nothing of it; let him ask the doctor, who will tell him something.4

Greet the Sisters for me, and believe me your

affectionate M. God bless you

1 In her last letter (of 25.11) Sr. A. Santina gives her good news about

the essential expenses for the house, among them the mattresses.

2 The Sisters, who always went in pairs to nurse the sick at home,

had to report to the Superior. The Mother advises her to receive these re-

ports more diligently. Moreover, she should avoid sending the same two Sisters

together to the sick too often. And further: let her be prudent and not re-

veal the faults of one of the two Sisters that the other may have told her.

3 It is good that she should go in person to see the sick and the Sisters'

service.

4 As for that gentleman. A lawyer – writes the Superior – had learnt

from Sr. A. Vincenza's sister that she suffered from asthma and that the air of Piacenza had

done her so much good that she was cured. He wants more precise information about this, because

his wife suffers from the same illness.

.

She writes to her at Foligno telling her to inform Countess Trotti on her way back, as the Countess was annoyed that Vincenza did not call on her. She will send Sr. A. Filomena to Ferrara with the teacher. She wants Vincenza to stop at least two days in Ferrara to put everything in order. She herself is in the most dreadful tribulations.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hope this finds you at Foligno, where I am addressing it. Listen, when you come back be sure to give Countess Trotti notice.1 My dear, if you knew how much trouble she has given me! She even telegraphed me that you had already passed through; in short, you cannot imagine all they invented; and she sent Signora Teresa,2 and I will not tell you all the things she said to me on the Countess's orders, a thousand silly things. Enough, all for God.

2. You must know that tomorrow I am sending Sr. A. Filomena with the teacher, who wants to try for a year and is a lay woman, since I did not want to clothe her.3 I have had all these things written to the Countess.

3. Sr. A. Giovannina4 wrote to me that the doctor has prescribed steam baths for the Sister and that a man is needed to load the apparatus; very well, the man yes, but not the nuns; I do not want them to go there. You will certainly be firmer than I am.5

4. I shall not write to you here again; I shall write to you at Ferrara, where I want you to stay two days to see everything and put it all in order. I received yours and was glad to hear so much good news, for amid the most dreadful tribulations that stifle me, I am

at the limit, one might say in an abyss; I do not know where my head is.

Goodbye, dear Vincenza, I long to embrace you. Believe me, in the depths of sorrow, yours for all ages.

Goodbye, affectionately, M.

1 be sure to give notice: inform.

2 Signora Teresa Zagotti, her secretary.

3 Tomorrow I am sending Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni to Ferrara to accom-

pany the teacher. She is still a lay woman, because she has not allowed her to take the reli-

gious habit.

4 Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno, the Superior of the Foligno house; the steam

baths for the sick Sister.

5 You will be firmer than I in having my wishes observed.

She cannot accept his request, since it is the Institute's practice to found houses with no fewer than four Sisters. She is willing to oblige him, but with the stated number.

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. I regret that I cannot accept your request, for the reason that we cannot go fewer than four, so I am sorry to have to withdraw, awaiting the time when Your Lordship may express your wish anew.1

2. Should you be unable to do without them for your Schools, do not hesitate to apply again, for we shall always be ready to come, with the number I have indicated.2

Please accept the sentiments of deep esteem of one who professes herself yours, Most Illustrious Sir,

[ROSA GATTORNO]

1 For the other requests for Sisters for schools too she had kept

firmly to this number.

2 She leaves the door open, while standing firm in her requirement.

She confesses that she is at the height of her tribulations and tries to bear everything with love. One must be patient and not lose heart. In the end death comes and seals everything; sweet is the thought of going to the feet of Jesus and entering His Kingdom without waiting in antechambers, having waited in so many in this world. She commends a Sister to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that Fr A... has been here; how angry he was... because you took the Sister from him! He told me you had told him to send her to you; is it true? Try to smooth things over so that he is not upset, because these are dreadful times for us.1 God wants to humble us, and I assure you I am now bearing a good dose of it; may the good God help me to bear everything for His love in holy resignation, for the flesh writhes under so cruel a martyrdom2 that never ends, nor can one see when it will end. Patience!

2. Take care of yourself, do not lose heart, for in the end death comes and everything is over; it seals every pain, and there remains for us the sweet thought of bringing it to the feet of Jesus in payment for our sins and of entering His kingdom without having to wait in the antechamber, having waited so much in this world at the doors of the great, what cold we suffered, what humiliations;3 in short, it seems to me that antechambers are very painful; and it would be too hard not to be able to enter quickly and embrace the One we love so much.

3. I have left Fr Accinelli F. 1,500 to pay the debts of

S. P. d'Arena; he has received a postulant and is sending her to me here.4 I urge you to keep a close watch on Sr. A. Domitilla, because her silence, her refusal to say anything, is very alarming; it means she is very much an accomplice; enough, I commend her to you.5

Goodbye, my dear daughter; tell me, when will you come? I am yours eternally,

M. R.

1 Fr Accinelli has been here: at Piacenza; how angry he was because you took

the Sister from him. The Superior Francesca, needing a nursing Sister

for the hospital, had taken her from the Genoa house, so that Fr Accinelli, in his

capacity as administrator of the house, had been annoyed. Try to smooth things over; Sr.

A. Francesca writes to M. Rosa on 1 December: “I cannot wait to see him

(Fr Accinelli) to tell him the reason”.

2 I am bearing a good dose of suffering, with great trust in God,

while feeling the weakness of the flesh. “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak”

(Mk 14:38b).

3 what cold we had to suffer, and what humiliation.

4 to pay the debts left at Sampierdarena by the former Superior Biagini;

he has received a postulant and is sending her to me here at Piacenza.

5 Sr. A. Domitilla, one of the Sisters of the Sampierdarena house, transferred

to the hospital after Biagini's flight; she stubbornly refuses to reveal anything

about the disorders that took place there, which means she is an accomplice. She commends her so that

she may be well formed and become a true Daughter of Saint Anne.

She is against visits home; Francesca must hold firmly to this wish of hers. She is to treat Fr Accinelli well. The Mother has given him the sum needed to pay off the debts. Once that is done, Francesca must manage the house's administration herself. She is to keep secret what the Mother tells her. She needs prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am answering at once your letter, which [I have] just finished reading. Listen, my dear daughter, stand firm and do not send any of them home; I do not want it, and you will say that it is my wish and order, that I wrote to you not to let any of them go. Too many muddles have happened. Enough, whoever goes never comes back; have a good dinner made for them and whatever else is needed.1

2. I am very pleased with what you tell me about the accounts. Yes, my dear, try to manage by yourself; you must know that I left F. 1,500 – fifteen hundred – because he told me there were many debts to pay, and so with this he can pay them; and then, when he has settled the large ones, you could carry on by yourself.2

3. Well done, be strong and courageous, for that is my only wish. I would not want anyone to read this letter or know what I am writing to you, because by it I mean to accede to your wishes.

4. I am sending you the book the teacher asked for; you cannot imagine what a consolation your letter was to me. Ah, dear daughter, have prayers said that I may not have to take the oaths!3 I am glad to hear of the girls' conduct and of providence. Blessed

be God, and may a thousand blessings descend on your head and on all your community. I am for ever your

affectionate M. R.

the resident girls to go to their families. Too many muddles have happened, too many dis-

orders. She alludes to the unpleasant events of which not only the Sisters but also the girls

were aware: cf. L 364, n. 1. With this prohibition the Mother wants to prevent news

from spreading and unpleasant rumours arising. Have... needed. Have a good

dinner prepared and whatever is needed for the Christmas feast.

house accounts (not Fr Accinelli); I have given him F. 1,500 (cf. L 375,3)

to pay the large debts; in this way things will be easier for you and you will be able to manage the

house's administration yourself.

The house at Foligno worries her, and she agrees with the Duchess not to take resident girls. The school for little boys and girls and the loom school are more than enough. Signora Biagini complains about her daughter Caterina. She must be told that, if Caterina was made Superior though young, she was well protected and guided, more than she is now. God permitted that the Mother should be slandered by this creature on whom so much kindness had been bestowed.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Last night I received your long letter, and I also received the other one written when you arrived at Foligno; you cannot imagine what worry this house gives me.2

2. I too agree with the Duchess not to take resident girls; you know, they drive one mad;3 so they have enough with a school for boys, one for girls and the looms I am sending you today.

3. Watch carefully, if you leave this Sister, Sr. A. Natalina, that she is not the one who carries tales and wants to play the Superior.4 I am thinking of changing the Superior, because if that is how things are she must be removed, otherwise there will always be new muddles.5

4. Pay the Father Guardian for his trip to Perugia when he went to see the place; work out how much is due and then pay him.6

5. I hear about Signora Biagini; well, tell her that I cannot know what her daughter took, since it is a house that lives on

providence, so it is hard to know; only that, not content with providing for herself, she provided also for the one she took with her;7 and if it was a crime to have made her Superior so young, let her know that among the Sisters of Charity themselves we have much younger Superiors; and indeed she is now a teacher in an infant school, and certainly, not yet being clothed, and in such places they are far more exposed than where she was, in a house that had dealings only with the Superiors and the Confessor, where she was very well watched over, with an older Sister. If the Confessor did such a thing, what is one to say?8

6. They cannot say I did not watch over her daughter well; that, no. Enough, God permitted that I should be so cruelly slandered with the most atrocious inventions by this creature on whom Saint Anne bestowed so much kindness. Enough, may His holy will be done.

7. You tell me you will write to the Inspector; no, my dear Vincenza, we are in order with the Inspector; only, if he should come, they have only to say that the teacher fell ill and had to leave, but will soon be replaced, which is the truth.9

8. Oh, if I find a strong and good Superior to send you, then you could come back here. Enough, let us pray; God wills it so; patience.

9. Goodbye. I am yours, not as you say in heaven, but close together, and I shall be content to be the footstool of the Daughters of Saint Anne. Ah, daughter of my affection, what am I to tell you? Let us only take comfort that no one can take our place in Heaven from us, and when we get there we shall rest for eternity.10

Yours on earth and in heaven,

affectionately, M. R. Carlotta sends her greetings.

2. Listen, for your guidance: when you go to Bologna the Countess will ask you many questions about Augusta.2 Answer that I have written nothing to you and that the mother has written me nothing about it; and stand firm, whatever she may say to you; firm. Accinelli told me it will be about 1,500; they filled their purses for the two of them, each having taken more than 600 francs straight away. And if she gives you any, take it, for it is our money.

affectionate M.

1. I have received your most esteemed letter of acceptance. I inform Your Most Illustrious Lordships that the four religious will be with you on the 28th of this month; two of them are the certified teachers, whose names are Marianna Morosini and Maria Sabatelli.1

She asks her to tell Signora Biagini that she has written to no one, neither in Turin nor elsewhere. Patience! This lie too will go to keep the others company. One must go forward with courage, loving God and bearing everything for Him. Advice for the nurses.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter and am answering at once so that you can tell Signora Biagini that I know nothing of the letters she speaks of; I have not written a word, neither to Turin nor anywhere else, and I have not said the least word about her, and I am very sorry that it is said I wrote; it is an outright falsehood.2

2. Patience! This one too will go to keep company with the other lies; this breed of sin has short legs and soon comes to a stop, unable to go any further, and shows its face uncovered; I am very glad that the rusty pot throws up its rusty iron as it boils; when they have finished, then we shall begin to rejoice with the Lord over the fine and gracious persecutions they procure for us.3

3. Forward, courage, for you have not wounded us yet, since our breast is of bronze; let them do and say what they will; mamma used to say that to shut the mouths of slanderers all the mud in the ditches of the Bisagno would not be enough.4

4. Let us love God and suffer everything for Him, to His honour and glory. The news you give me is an immense consolation.5

5. Dear Jesus, bless my dear daughter and give her the strength of a giant and the love of a seraph.

Goodbye; I fear this will no longer find you there. Yours eternally,

affectionately, Sr. A. ROSA

6. Listen, a thought came to me, and indeed occupied me a good deal; do you know about what? about dressing those ugly diseases we talked of; listen, my opinion is this: that they should assist when the doctor dresses them, that is fine, but I would say no to their dressing them alone; there is, however, one exception: when the diseases are sent by God, then they may dress them alone too; when they are caused by sin, then they must only assist when the doctor dresses them, provided it is only one person. We have already put this in the book we have had printed, which I hope to send you soon.6 I shall tell you why in person; it is quite right; I thought about it a whole night.

Goodbye, your

affectionate M.

4 Some girls at the “Istituto S. Anna” at Sampierdarena were unwell.

Her thoughts often turn to the two runaways: cf. L 367, n. 3.

5 One of the two, Tecla, has written imploring her to take her back (cf. L

379,3). She had returned to the Daughters of Charity in Turin and cannot stay there.

6 The other: Caterina Biagini seems to be going home: cf. L 383, n. 2.

7 She may tell the Sisters; it will be a lesson to them.

8 She fears that Biagini too may write asking to be taken back.

9 In the Sampierdarena House things are bad, there are still difficulties, and this one

(Tecla) asks me to go back there...

10 This C.: it may be taken as this House or, more fittingly, this one,

Carlotta (Sr. A. C. Biagini, sister of Caterina, formerly Sr. A. Augusta).

She wishes him heavenly consolations for the birth of Jesus. She asks why he did not give the postulant the indulgenced crucifix he obtained for her. She asks him to look after a seminarian who must sit the examination for admission to priestly Ordination.

A.M.F. My Father,

1. What am I to say to you for the coming of the Child? May He bring you a new year full of every kind of heavenly consolation; not earthly ones, for we poor religious want nothing from the earth, and it can give us nothing that pleases us; all we have of it is a pig of a body, which we shall leave to it.1

2. My Father, I thought you had given the postulant my crucifix, which you wrote was so well furnished with blessings and relics; why do you not send it to me? I am still without one.2

3. Listen, now I would like you to take up another matter and answer me at once. It concerns a young man who failed the examinations for admission to Ordination, and the Parish Priest, who has kept him in his house for ten years..., and the reason he was failed is that they fear, since he is very gifted, that the said Parish Priest will put him at the head of the Congregation he wants to found.3

4. So this Parish Priest intends to send him to receive Ordination in Rome, submitting to a new examination. Please answer me at once, telling me how he

should proceed and what he should take with him. For charity's sake, try to see that he achieves his aim. Poor young man, he is so overcome by melancholy that it is pitiful. My Father, see to it, because I have given my word. Write to me at once.

5. I would like you also to tell me something about the Nizza papers, which torment me not a little,4 and also about the paper from the Parish Priest of S. Ippolito, also of Nizza. My Father, how much trouble this nuisance gives you! But if I do not manage to be useful on earth, I promise to be so in heaven. Write to me at once and believe me your poor one, yes, but always, for life,

your affectionate Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 all we have... leave to it: an expression reflecting a certain mentality

of the time.

2 The postulant Maria Capoferri, of Rome, had entered on 19 December. She

thought he had given her the Crucifix (cf. L 338,2).

3 The Parish Priest is Fr Giovanni Boffetti, who wrote to her from Vespolate (NO)

asking her to help “the young man of very fine intellect and upright and holy con-

duct... who is master = teacher of the sons of the nascent institute”. The Congregation

the Parish Priest wishes to found is called in that letter: Sons of Saint Anne.

4 the Nizza papers: cf. L 385, n. 2.

She wishes her a happy Christmas and New Year. She sends some things for Rosa's dear family, in thanksgiving for a grace received and so that they may pray for other graces: Father Tornatore's readmission and a favourable outcome of the Ricchini lawsuit. She is weighed down with sorrows, but suffering is sweet to her. She commends herself to Anna's prayers and awaits a reply.

A.M.F.

My Anna,

1. I wish you happy holidays, with greetings for holy Christmas and a happy New Year.

2. I am sending you some things for my dear jewels, Rosa's family;1 they are all new and from a healthy person, they may be sure. Part of these things is for the good journey I had when I left Genoa, and the rest because I want a grace I am expecting in these days. For pity's sake, let them pray that I may obtain it; it concerns, as you well know, that person's readmission.2

3. Listen, tell them to pray that I may not have to take the oaths I must soon go to take; the lawsuit, that I may win it. You cannot imagine the distress I am in.3 By God's grace I am tormented on every side; it is a fierce war.

4. I will say nothing of my health; it is failing badly and I am always suffering a great deal, but very willingly, and I cling as closely as I can to this sweet suffering. Pray, for pity's sake; obtain for me what you see is so very necessary. Pray, for now Satan is making every effort.

5. Tell me something, if you write to me as I hope, that you will tell me I shall have everything; at least these two things I mention I shall know; my Rosa makes me hope so; and what do you say?

6. Give the letter to the Superior at Genoa, so that it is sure to reach me; I am waiting for it.4

Goodbye; pray, for pity's sake.

Yours for ever, affectionately, M. R. GATTORNO

If I obtain everything, I shall send more things to the dear family.

1 My dear jewels: the family of Rosa Parodi, fatherless and very poor,

but rich in faith. Mother Rosa helps them when she can. She prays and asks

her “seraph Rosa” to pray too. (Cf. 178,1).

2 that Fr Tornatore be readmitted to the Institute. This is a grace she had long

been asking of the Lord, praying and having others pray and sending letters and peti-

tions to influential persons. (Cf. L 134, n. 2).

3 oaths... lawsuit: cf. L 355, n. 2.

4 The Superior of the Genoa house, Sr. A. Santina Solenghi.

She is delighted to hear they have many sick to care for. She asks her to take a letter and a parcel to Anna Grasso. Sr. A. Tecla has written imploring to be taken back, but that will never be.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. My daughter, I have always received your letters and see that you have many sick people; I am very, very glad and bless God for being so good to His daughters.

2. Listen, the Superior of the Hospital will give you a bundle, and you will take it to Anna Grasso. She knows what to do with it; and take this letter, which you will find enclosed, together with it. I hope you will do everything well.1

Meanwhile, being in a hurry, I end by wishing you all a thousand blessings from heaven, as I am your

affectionate M. R. G.

3. Today I received a letter from Sr. A. Tecla,2 in which she im-

plores me to take her back and put her at S. P. d'Arena for the school, even

dressed as a lay woman; in short, she says so many things, but it will never be

that an apostate is readmitted. She says she had to

leave because she could not bear to stay in that institute and that she had

such great remorse that she could not live. How dreadful! You may tell

the Sisters; it will be a lesson to them.

1 Cf. L 389.

2 The Sister who fled from the Sampierdarena house. Cf. L 387,5-6.

She sends the Rules ad experimentum and asks a blessing for the Superiors, who are to form the Sisters in their spirit and in perfect observance. The prophecy of the holy Pope Pius IX is being fulfilled. She offers her good wishes and asks for his pastoral blessing.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. A holy duty obliges me to send you our little Rules, just printed with the permission of the Sacred Congregation, as a trial, so as to test whether they are suited to continuing our present way of working and our customs. By God's mercy, so far everything has been done with the greatest scrupulousness.1

2. Most Reverend Eminence, bless all the Superiors, who must instil the spirit of these Constitutions well, so that they may reach perfect observance.

3. Our houses now number twenty-four, and we have besides an infinity of requests, so that I do not know how to satisfy the Bishops.2

4. This year the poor nurses have had the good fortune to see many conversions and retractions; what the Holy Father told me the first time I was at his Feet is coming true: that they will be so many apostles spreading throughout the world. Oh, great holy Pope Pius IX!

5. Forgive me for dwelling on an account of God's Work, but as I am accustomed to do so every year,3 I cannot live in peace unless I lay all that happens in it at the feet of my Superior.

6. The wishes that in these holy days this wretched Servant of yours

offers for the prosperity of Your Most Reverend Eminence are more fervent than usual, as I beg the Child Jesus to fulfil all your desires.

Please grant your pastoral blessing to the whole Institute, and also to one who, prostrate at your Feet, signs herself with the deepest veneration

Your Most Reverend Eminence's humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Our little Rules. They had been printed by the F. Solari press, Pia-

cenza, with the closing note of the Cardinal Protector. One must point out the Mother's

inaccuracy in attributing to the permission of the Sacred Congregation what

was simply a concession by Cardinal Vannicelli in his capacity as

Protector. The note reads: “Without prejudice to the authoritative approval of the Holy

Apostolic See, on which the sanction of these rules depends, considering

the order with which the nascent Institute called the

Daughters of Saint Anne proceeds in every respect, already spread in various places; bearing in mind the various ways in which

it renders service in the continual exercise of works of Charity towards every class

of persons, but especially the poor and sick, for Our part, by way of

experiment, the printing of the said rules is permitted”.

2 The houses actually open number 24, and negotiations were under way for others.

3 Cf. Lettere 2, L 4; 335; Lettere 3, L 139, and the present one. She had also written to him

on other occasions to ask for help and advice.

Although she had the Sisters ready, through a misunderstanding she did not notify him; she apologizes and declares herself willing to withdraw if they wish to turn to another Institute.

[Reverend Archpriest]1

1. I have received your most esteemed letter, which I answer by return of post. I see from it that you were expecting a reply from me; I have yours saying that, provided I bring a teacher of higher grade, our coming is fixed for the second of January.2

2. I am deeply sorry to have failed in this duty through a misunderstanding, and that the Most Honourable Council has been displeased, when I had everything ready to come.3

3. Now, to my great regret, I leave Your Most Illustrious Lordships free to turn to another Institute, where you will certainly find better candidates than us.

Please be so good as to send me the two certificates4 and accept the sentiments of esteem and respect

of your Reverend Lordship's most humble Sr. A. R. G.

1 The Archpriest is Fr Pietro Tamagni. Cf. L 380.

2 The Congregation was expecting a further reply from her,

whereas she considered the Sisters' coming on the second of January definitely settled,

in accordance with the arrangements made with the Reverend Tamagni.

3 She takes the blame for the misunderstanding and withdraws from the commitment.

4 She asks for the return of the two certificates sent.

She thanks her for the letters and gifts and rejoices at the welcome they received from the Archbishop. Glory to the Eternal Father! She loves Him so much that every pain is a delight to her. On Christmas Day she was very ill. Tecla insists on being readmitted. They will see what to decide.

A.M.F.

My beloved Francesca,

1. I received your gifts and letters from the Sister; too much; I would not want you to have deprived yourself to send me so many things. Your letter gave me immense pleasure, the one I received this morning, as did the one I received from the Sisters' hands.

2. How glad I am of the welcome the Archbishop gave you! Yes, glory to God our Father.1

3. Ah, dear Francesca, how dear is my Eternal Father, all mine, the much beloved! Ah, if you came [to] love Him as I love Him, you would certainly no longer know what suffering means; every pain would be a delight to you, knowing that by this means one comes to taste His delicious love.2

4. Yesterday I suffered a great deal; I fainted several times, my lung was moving like a potato, the headache was a treat. I forced myself to get up to keep the Father company during his dinner,3 but what can I say, there was a duet: Sr. A. Benedetta was crying, Carlottina too, and I put on as lively a face as I could; but at 4 I had a fine fainting fit and suffered, God alone knows how much. Enough, I had Sr. A. Vincenza with me.

5. Today letters from Tecla again; what do you say? If you heard how she writes! Yes, I really pity her, but on the other hand it tears me apart to hear her. Enough, tomorrow we shall consult a little and see.4

Goodbye, your affectionate

[M. ROSA]

1 The Archbishop had received both her and the Superior Eli-

sabetta kindly and had taken an interest in both communities. Sr. A. Francesca had

invited him to visit the hospital.

2 In Mgr Magnasco's charitable gesture and his interest in the

two communities of Genoa and Sampierdarena the Mother sees a sign of the

change in his heart towards God's Work, and from the depths of her

soul there springs spontaneous thanksgiving to the Eternal Father for this grace obtained by

insistent and trusting prayer.

3 On Christmas Day she had invited Fr Tornatore to dinner at the Mother

House.

4 Tecla. Cf. L 390,3. She feels great pity for her. She wants to talk about it with the Father. Re-

garding Tecla, Sr. A. Francesca replied on 28 December: “I hear what you say about Te-

cla; it pains me; it seems to me she can be taken back, but you decide, because you know

things better than I do; certainly it is a soul rescued from

sin, because if she stays outside, who knows where she will end up”.

Yes, the Sisters will go to Mercatello, but in January, so she needs people; she will send two at once, who will go to Lugo, and then the other two. She is writing to Fr Accinelli about it. Francesca wrote that she fears boring her by talking about God. Oh no! she delights in it so much that not even a day and a night would satisfy her hunger for knowledge of Him. Let her speak of Him; she will never go wrong in doing so; let her love and she will become a saint. She suffers from the cold at Piacenza, but work has prevented her from going to Sampierdarena or to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You ask me in your letter whether they are still going to Mercatello;2 yes, but it has been fixed for 10 January and I need people; look around in Genoa; it seems to me that Sr. A. Marta, you know, the one from Ferrara, did the third class, and there is Sr. A. Stanislaa, she too. I would need these two at once, but I would not want to put Sr. A. Marta together with Stanislaa; if you see that there is someone of good appearance, send her to me together with Sr. A. Marta, and so there would be two, whom I need at once for Lugo; so writes Sr. A. Vincenza, who has been there since the 28th of this month, and I would need them at once.3

2. I am now writing to Fr Accinelli so that he will not be upset, for I shall send him three much better, sturdier and older ones;4 so you will send Sr. A. Stanislaa together with Sr. A. Battistina; then I shall take no one else from the Hospital, because in this way they gain a little more experience, and certainly I shall soon be able to have some for another hospital.5

3. Listen, until the 9th you may keep Sr. A. Battistina with you, and Sr. A. Stanislaa too, but you must send me the two at once, because Sr. A. Vincenza is waiting for them.

4. You tell me you fear that by lingering with me to speak of God you might bore me. Ah, dear daughter! If I found a creature who merely spoke to me of Him to give me a little pleasure, I assure you that if they spoke to me of Him for a whole night and a day, they would only kindle in me the desire to hear more and more. Ah, who will ever satisfy me? No one, only You, my God, in Your beatitude.6

5. Always speak to me of Jesus, for you will never go wrong, and I shall read your letters with keen pleasure. Love, yes, love, for whoever comes [to] love can no longer sin; whoever does not sin becomes a saint; and once a saint, enjoys the immense good that is God. Ah, there is no good above You, good of all good, treasure of all treasures.7

6. Goodbye; today I am out of bed, but the cold of Piacenza is clearly not for one who has no blood or life in her, as I am. Enough, let us hope I can hold out. Were it not [for] the great affairs and the Ricchini lawsuit,8 I would have come to spend the winter with you, or in Rome; but patience is needed! Goodbye, your

affectionate M. for all ages. Amen.

1 The Mother is replying to Francesca's letter of 28 December.

2 You ask me. The Mother had not mentioned it again, because there had been a mis-

understanding about it. Cf. L 392.

3 As usual, when she needs Sisters for houses to be opened, she con-

sults in order to find suitable persons.

4 I am writing to Fr Accinelli so that he will not be upset (cf. L 375,1 and the relevant note).

I shall send him... older in vocation.

5 in this way they gain experience, are formed and acquire competence, and so will be

ready for a new hospital.

6 You tell me... Sr. A. Francesca had candidly opened her heart and

ended with an anguished question revealing a burning desire:

“so what must I do to love Jesus? Tell me, for I am resolved to do it

at any cost; forgive me for having dwelt so long on my

miseries”. At this point the Mother reveals the ardour of her desire for God, which becomes

a never-satisfied thirst for knowledge of Him and an unbridgeable distance. Who will ever

satisfy (fill) me? God alone, in the full enjoyment of heaven.

7 She asks her beloved Francesca, one of her dearest daughters, always to speak to her

of Jesus, and draws her to her side on the way of love with vigour and strength: love, yes,

love; and dispels her doubts and hesitations: “I do not know how to make this act of aban-

doning myself into God's hands; I desire it, but a strong apprehension makes me

fall back into my usual fear”, and she shows her the way of maturity, which is fullness of obla-

tion (whoever comes to love can no longer sin) and the attainment of the purpose of

human existence: the enjoyment of the immense good that is God.

8 Fr Ricchini. Cf. L 355, n. 2.

?

She has written to Genoa to have the two religious destined for Lugo sent off. She is sorry Vincenza will not be at Piacenza for New Year. She puts forward her plan: since the Sisters must be at Mercatello on 10 January, it would be good for Vincenza to meet them at Pesaro and accompany them.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. Here I am, up and better. I hear what you tell me in your letter received yesterday, the second since you have been at Lugo.1 I wrote at once to Genoa to send me two religious who can read and write well; one is Sr. A. Marta, you know her, who said she did the third class, and the other someone who can barely read and write; as soon as they send them to me I shall send them to you.2

2. I hear you cannot come for New Year's Day; patience!

3. Listen, the people of Mercatello have written begging us to go there, and they accept us on our terms.3 You see, if you could hear what a courteous letter it is! So I have fixed 10 January; it seems to me I could send the Sisters to meet you, and you could all meet at Pesaro, and so you would spare yourself a useless journey,4 because from your letter I see you will have to stay there some days more, and the 10th will soon come. What do you say?

4. The Countess,5 you know, wrote to me in her own hand; we are at the stage of endearments. Let us hope it lasts. See whether the Superior wears mittens, and if so say something to her, and tell her we may not wear them. Alas, if she is so delicate, how dread-

ful! I am afraid she will not do well and is too delicate. For charity's sake, be watchful.7 Goodbye, for I have so much to write. I am yours eternally,

affectionately, M. R.

1 what you tell me: she describes the cordial welcome and the large house, the

school, the chapel.

2 She has written to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa. Cf. L 394,1.

3 There had been some difficulty about the Sisters' qualifications. Cf.

L 392.

4 I could send you the Sisters destined for Mercatello, having them leave so

that you all meet at Pesaro, and so you would avoid travelling as far as Piacenza.

5 Countess Maria Anna Trotti.

6 see whether, find out if the Superior, Sr. A. Edvige Moroncini,

wears mittens (fingerless gloves), and tell her that we do not wear them.

7 Replying the next day, Sr. A. Vincenza writes: “you are not mis-

taken in saying she is delicate; she goes round the house with a foot-warmer in her hand, and mind,

it is not cold”.
